tasks.taskName: Lesson: Evaluating Websites: Is It True?
tasks.content: Not everything found on the internet is accurate, up to date, or true, so it is an important skill to be able to evaluate a website, which means judging carefully whether we should trust the information on it. One helpful thing to check is who wrote or published the website, because information from a well-known, trusted organisation, such as a museum, a government website, or a respected news source, is usually more reliable than a website with no named author at all. It is also helpful to check when a website was last updated, because some information, especially facts about current events or fast-changing topics, can quickly become out of date. Another useful strategy is to compare the same piece of information across two or three different trusted websites, because if several reliable sources agree, the information is more likely to be accurate. We should also be alert to websites that seem to be trying to sell us something, or that use exaggerated claims and dramatic language, because this can be a sign that the information is biased or not entirely truthful. If we are ever unsure whether a website can be trusted, the best thing to do is ask a trusted adult or teacher, who can help us decide together whether the information is reliable.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A digital footprint is the trail of information left behind by everything we do online, such as messages we send, photographs we post, comments we make, and websites we visit. Just like footprints left in sand can show where someone has walked, our digital footprint can show what we have done and said on the internet, and importantly, this trail can sometimes be seen by other people, and can be very difficult to completely remove once it exists. It is important to think carefully before posting or sharing anything online, because even things that feel private at the time, such as a photograph shared with what seems like only a few friends, could potentially be copied, shared further, or seen by people we did not expect. A helpful habit is to pause and think before posting, and ask ourselves whether we would be comfortable with a trusted adult, a teacher, or even a future employer seeing it one day. We should never post personal details, such as our address or school, and we should always ask a trusted adult before sharing photographs or videos of ourselves online. Being thoughtful about our digital footprint now helps protect our privacy and reputation, both today and in the future.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Animation is the process of making still pictures appear to move, by showing a fast sequence of slightly different images, one after another. This works because our eyes and brain blend the quick series of images together, creating the illusion of smooth movement, a trick that has been used in cartoons and films for many years. In digital animation, we often build this effect using frames, where each frame is a single image, and playing many frames quickly, one after another, makes the animation appear to move smoothly. In simple block-based coding, we can create animation using costumes, which are different versions of a character, and switching between costumes quickly using a loop can make a character appear to walk, jump, or flap its wings. For example, a program might say: repeat 10 times: switch to next costume, wait a fraction of a second. Another common animation technique is changing a character's position slightly, over and over again, in a loop, to make it appear to glide smoothly across the screen. Good animation usually needs small, careful changes between each frame or costume, because if the change between images is too large, the movement can look jumpy rather than smooth. Planning an animation, such as sketching the key positions first, helps make the final movement look believable.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Combining Software Tools for a Project
tasks.content: Many real projects on a computer are made by combining several different software tools together, rather than using just one program on its own. For example, imagine creating a project about the water cycle for the whole class to see. We might use a drawing program to create pictures of clouds, rain, and rivers, a word processing program to write clear explanations, and a slideshow program to bring the pictures and writing together into an organised, easy to follow presentation. Combining tools like this lets us use each program for the job it does best, such as using a drawing tool for illustrations and a word processor for detailed writing, rather than trying to force one single program to do every single job. When combining tools, it is important to plan first, deciding what each part of the finished project will need, such as which pictures are required, how much text each slide should have, and in what order everything should appear. It also helps to keep our files organised in clearly named folders, so we can find the pictures, documents, and slides easily when we need to bring them all together. Learning to combine software tools thoughtfully helps us create polished, well-organised projects that communicate our ideas clearly and effectively.

levels.levelName: The Scratch Interface: Stage, Sprites, Blocks

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Scratch Interface: Stage, Sprites, Blocks
tasks.content: This year, we are moving up to a real, powerful coding program used by millions of kids around the world: Scratch! Scratch was created to help young people learn to code by snapping together colorful blocks, and today we will explore its main parts. The first important part is the stage, which is the rectangle in the corner of the screen where your project actually plays, showing the sprites, the background, and any action happening. Next are sprites, the characters or objects in your project, like a cat, a dragon, or a basketball, each one able to move, talk, and follow its own code. Every sprite you add appears in the sprite list, usually below the stage, where you can click on any sprite to work on its code. The last major part is the blocks palette, found on the left side of the screen, which holds every single block you could possibly use, organized into colorful categories like Motion, which is blue, Looks, which is purple, Sound, which is a pinkish color, Events, which is yellow, Control, which is orange, and more. To build a program, you drag blocks from the palette into the large white coding area in the middle of the screen, snapping them together like puzzle pieces to build a sequence. Learning where everything lives in Scratch, the stage, the sprite list, the blocks palette, and the coding area, will make everything else we learn this year much easier. Today we will take a guided tour of the Scratch interface, clicking on different parts and predicting what each one is used for before we try it ourselves.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Motion Blocks: Making Sprites Move
tasks.content: Motion blocks are the blue blocks in Scratch, and they control everything about how a sprite moves and where it faces. Some of the most common motion blocks include "move 10 steps," which moves a sprite forward in the direction it is currently facing, "turn right 15 degrees" and "turn left 15 degrees," which rotate the sprite, and "go to x: 0 y: 0," which instantly teleports a sprite to a specific spot on the stage. Scratch uses a coordinate system to describe exact positions on the stage, using two numbers called x and y. The x number tells how far left or right a sprite is, and the y number tells how far up or down it is, with the very center of the stage being x: 0, y: 0. Understanding coordinates helps us place sprites exactly where we want them, instead of just guessing. Another useful motion block is "glide 1 second to x: ___ y: ___," which moves a sprite smoothly to a new spot over time, instead of jumping there instantly, which can make animations look much more natural. If a sprite ever points in a direction that seems upside down or sideways after turning, we can use the "point in direction" block to fix it and set it facing exactly the way we want. Motion blocks are often combined with loops, letting a sprite move forward repeatedly to travel a long distance, or bounce back and forth across the stage. Today we will experiment with different motion blocks, testing how numbers change a sprite's movement, and we will use coordinates to guide a sprite to a specific target spot on the stage.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Loop Blocks: Repeat and Forever
tasks.content: In Scratch, loop blocks live in the orange Control category, and they help us repeat actions without writing the same blocks again and again. We already know about the repeat block, which repeats whatever blocks are snapped inside it a certain number of times, like "repeat 10." But Scratch also has another very important loop called the forever block, which repeats whatever is inside it endlessly, without ever stopping on its own, until the project is stopped completely. The forever block is extremely useful for things that should always be happening, like a sprite that should always follow the mouse pointer around the stage, or a background that should always slowly change color throughout the entire project. However, we need to be careful with forever blocks, because anything placed after a forever block in a sequence will actually never run, since the forever loop never finishes on its own to let the program continue! This is different from a repeat block, which does eventually finish after its set number of repeats, allowing the program to continue on to whatever comes next. Choosing between repeat and forever depends entirely on what we want our project to do. If we want an action to happen an exact number of times, like a character taking exactly five steps, we use repeat. If we want something to keep happening for as long as the project is running, like a spinning windmill in the background, we use forever. Today we will experiment with both repeat and forever blocks, comparing what happens when we place blocks after each one, and we will decide which loop fits different project ideas best.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Event Blocks: When Green Flag Clicked

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Event Blocks: When Green Flag Clicked
tasks.content: Event blocks in Scratch are yellow, hat-shaped blocks that sit at the very top of a sequence, and they decide exactly when the blocks underneath them will start running. The most common event block in Scratch is "when green flag clicked," which starts the attached code the moment someone clicks the green flag icon above the stage, which is how almost every Scratch project begins. Another important event block is "when this sprite clicked," which only runs its code when someone clicks directly on that particular sprite, not the whole project. Scratch also has "when key pressed," which lets us choose a specific keyboard key, like the space bar or an arrow key, so the code underneath only runs when that exact key is pressed. There is also a broadcast-related event, "when I receive," which we will learn much more about very soon, that starts code when a message is sent from somewhere else in the project. Every single script, which is what we call a connected stack of blocks, needs an event block at the top, or it will never run at all, no matter how perfectly the rest of the blocks are built! This is an important rule to remember: without an event, blocks just sit in the coding area, doing nothing. A single Scratch project can, and usually does, have many different scripts, each starting with its own event block, allowing many different things to happen depending on what the person playing the project actually does. Today we will build several small scripts, each starting with a different event block, and test how each one behaves differently.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Sound Blocks: Adding Music and Effects
tasks.content: Sound blocks in Scratch are a pinkish-magenta color, and they let us add music, sound effects, and audio to our projects, making them feel much more exciting and alive. One common sound block is "play sound until done," which plays a chosen sound and waits for it to completely finish before moving on to the next block in the script. There is also "start sound," which plays a sound but does not wait, letting the rest of the script keep running at the very same time as the sound plays, which is useful when you want a sprite to move and make noise simultaneously. Scratch comes with a large sound library full of ready-made sound effects, like a pop, a meow, or drum beats, and you can also record your own sounds using a microphone, or upload sound files from your computer! Sound blocks also let us adjust volume, using a block like "change volume by," and we can even add fun effects, like "set pitch effect," which can make a sound sound higher or lower, almost like a cartoon character's voice. Adding well-chosen sound to a project can completely change how it feels: imagine a spooky Halloween scene with eerie sound effects, compared to the very same scene with cheerful, bouncy music instead, it would feel like a totally different project! It is important to choose sounds that match the mood and story of your project, rather than just picking random sounds. Today we will explore the built-in sound library, test the difference between "play sound until done" and "start sound," and add at least one sound effect to a sprite's script.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: So far, every script we have built runs the exact same way every single time. But real programs, like games, often need to make decisions, doing different things depending on what is happening. That is where the if-then block comes in! The if-then block is found in the Control category, and it checks whether something is true or false. If the condition inside the block is true, the blocks snapped inside it will run. If the condition is false, those blocks are simply skipped, and the script continues on without them. For example, imagine a game where a cat sprite should say "You found it!" only if it touches a treasure sprite. We could build this using an if-then block: "if touching treasure, then say You found it!" If the cat is not touching the treasure, nothing happens, the cat stays quiet, and the game keeps going normally. The condition inside an if-then block often uses special blocks shaped like hexagons, like "touching \_\_?" or "key pressed?", which return either true or false depending on what is currently happening in the project. If-then blocks are usually placed inside a forever loop, so the computer keeps checking the condition over and over again, watching for exactly the right moment for it to become true, like constantly checking whether the cat has touched the treasure yet. Making decisions with if-then blocks is a huge step up from everything we have learned so far, because it lets our projects respond differently depending on what is actually happening, instead of always doing the exact same thing. Today we will build a script using an if-then block inside a forever loop, testing what happens when the condition is true compared to when it is false.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Introduction to Variables: Keeping Score
tasks.content: A variable is like a labeled box that stores a piece of information a program needs to remember and can change over time. In Scratch, variables show up as orange blocks, and one of the most common uses for a variable is keeping score in a game! Let's say we want to build a simple game where a sprite earns a point every time it touches a coin sprite. First, we would create a variable, maybe named "score," and set it to 0 at the very beginning of the game, using a "set score to 0" block. Then, inside an if-then block that checks whether the sprite is touching the coin, we would add a "change score by 1" block, which adds one point to the score every single time the condition becomes true. Scratch can even show the current value of a variable right on the stage, like a little scoreboard in the corner, which updates automatically every time the variable changes, without us needing to do anything extra. Variables are not just for scores, they can store all kinds of information a program needs to remember, like a player's name, the number of lives left, or how much time is remaining. The important thing to understand about a variable is that its value can change while the program is running, unlike a fixed number that always stays the same. This is what makes variables so powerful: they let our projects remember and react to what has happened so far. Today we will create a score variable, set it to 0 at the start, and use a "change score by 1" block combined with an if-then block to build a very simple point-scoring game.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Now that our Scratch projects are getting more complex, with motion, loops, events, sounds, if-then blocks, and variables all working together, debugging becomes even more important, and even more interesting! When a Scratch project does not behave the way we expect, there are several strategies we can use to find the problem. First, we can click on individual blocks, or small groups of blocks, directly in the coding area, which runs just that part of the script by itself, helping us narrow down exactly where the problem might be hiding. Second, we can check our event blocks: is there an event block at the top of every script, and is it the right kind of event? Third, we can look closely at any if-then blocks: is the condition actually checking the right thing, like the correct sprite name or the correct variable? Fourth, we can watch variables on the stage while the project runs, checking whether they are changing the way we expect, like whether a score variable is actually going up when it should. A very common Scratch bug happens when a forever loop is missing, causing an if-then block to only check its condition one single time instead of continuously watching for it. Another common bug happens when blocks are snapped to the wrong sprite's script instead of the sprite we intended. Debugging in Scratch is a lot like being a detective: we gather clues, like what we expected to happen compared to what actually happened, and we test small changes one at a time, instead of changing many things at once, which can make it confusing to tell what actually fixed the problem. Today we will debug several sample projects with common Scratch mistakes already built in, working through each one using the strategies from this lesson.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: It's time to bring together everything we have learned this year, motion, loops, events, sound, if-then blocks, and variables, to design our very own simple game in Scratch! Designing a game starts with an idea, not with blocks. Before opening Scratch, good game designers think through some important questions: What is the goal of the game? How does the player control what happens? What makes the player win, or lose? For example, let's design a simple catching game: a basket sprite moves left and right using arrow key events, while an apple sprite falls from the top of the stage using motion blocks inside a loop. If the apple touches the basket, we use an if-then block to increase a score variable and reset the apple back to the top. If the apple reaches the bottom of the stage without touching the basket, the game could end, or a lives variable could go down by one instead. Notice how this one simple game idea actually uses almost everything we learned this year: events to control the basket, loops to keep the apple falling and the game running, if-then blocks to check for touching, and variables to track score. When designing your own game, it helps to start simple, get one basic part working first, like making the apple fall, before adding more complicated parts, like scoring and losing. This is exactly how professional game designers work too, building and testing one piece at a time instead of trying to build the whole game all at once. Today we will sketch a simple game idea on paper, listing which Scratch blocks we think we will need, before starting to build it step by step in Scratch.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: What a huge year of learning! You explored the Scratch interface, used motion blocks to move sprites, learned the difference between repeat and forever loops, used event blocks to control when scripts start, added sound and music to your projects, made decisions with if-then blocks, tracked information with variables, practiced debugging Scratch projects, and even designed your own simple game. Today's mini project is your chance to show off everything you have learned by building a complete small game or interactive project from start to finish. Begin with planning: sketch your idea on paper first, deciding on your sprites, your background, your goal, and how the player will control what happens. Think carefully about which events will start different parts of your project, whether you need a repeat loop or a forever loop, where an if-then block could check for something important, like touching another sprite, and whether a variable, like a score or a counter, would make your project more interesting. As you build, remember the debugging strategies we practiced: test small pieces as you go instead of waiting until the very end, click on small groups of blocks to check exactly what they do, and watch your variables while the project runs to make sure they behave the way you expect. If something is not working, take a breath, think like a detective, and look for clues about what is actually happening compared to what you expected. Once your project works, share it with a partner or the class, and try out a few other classmates' projects too, noticing how everyone combined the very same tools, motion, loops, events, sound, if-then blocks, and variables, in completely different and creative ways. You are becoming real Scratch programmers, and next year we will go even further with your skills!
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Modal verbs go before another verb to show how possible, certain or necessary something is. 'Might' and 'could' show something is only possible, 'should' can show advice or likelihood, and 'must' shows strong certainty or obligation. Choosing a different modal verb changes how confident a sentence sounds: compare 'It might rain' with 'It must rain' — the second sounds far more certain.

tasks.content: Across a whole text, not just within one paragraph, writers use cohesion devices to keep ideas connected. Pronouns like 'it', 'this' and 'they' refer back to something mentioned earlier, avoiding repetition, while adverbials such as 'consequently' or 'nevertheless' link paragraphs together by showing a result or a contrast. Deliberately repeating a key word can also remind the reader of the main idea running through a text.

tasks.content: Register means how formal or informal a piece of writing is, and choosing the right register depends on your audience and purpose. tasks.content: Etymology is the study of where words come from, and many English words originate from Latin and Greek. tasks.content: Percent means 'out of 100', so a decimal can be changed to a percentage by multiplying by 100: 0.25 = 25%. tasks.content: Tamil verbs change their ending to show kaalam (காலம், tense): past, present, and future. tasks.content: Different animal groups have very different life cycles: a mammal, like a human or a dog, is born live and grows through stages to adulthood, while an amphibian, like a frog, begins as an egg, hatches into a swimming tadpole, and metamorphoses into an adult that can live on land. An insect, like a butterfly, goes through complete metamorphosis, changing from egg to larva to pupa to adult, and a bird, like a robin, hatches from an egg and is fed by its parents until it can fly. Living things also reproduce in different ways: many animals reproduce sexually, where a male and female parent are needed, while some plants can also reproduce using seeds formed after pollination, or grow new plants from runners or bulbs.
Let's practice what we just learned!

After birth, a baby grows through infancy and early childhood, developing quickly in size and ability, before becoming a child and then reaching adolescence, or puberty, when the body changes rapidly to become an adult body. Adulthood is the longest stage of the human life cycle, during which the body is fully grown, before people eventually reach old age, when the body gradually becomes less able to do the things it once could.

A lever, like a seesaw or a pair of scissors, is a rigid bar that pivots around a fixed point called a fulcrum, allowing a small push to lift a heavier load. A pulley uses a wheel and rope to change the direction of a force, making it easier to lift heavy objects, such as raising a flag up a flagpole, while gears are toothed wheels that lock together so that turning one gear turns another, changing the speed or direction of movement, as seen in a bicycle's gears.

tasks.content: Some changes to materials are reversible, meaning the material can be changed back to how it was before, such as melting ice, which can be frozen again, or dissolving salt in water, which can be recovered by evaporating the water. Other changes are irreversible, meaning a new material is formed and the change cannot be undone, such as burning wood to make ash and smoke, baking a cake from raw ingredients, or an iron nail rusting when it reacts with oxygen and water. Mixing vinegar with bicarbonate of soda is a good classroom example of an irreversible change, because it creates new substances and produces bubbles of gas.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Repetition and Loops: Going Deeper
tasks.content: We already know that a loop repeats a group of instructions, but this year we look more closely at different types of loops and how to choose the right one for a task. A count-controlled loop, such as repeat 10 times, runs a set number of times that we decide in advance, and is useful when we already know exactly how many repetitions we need, such as drawing a shape with a known number of sides. A condition-controlled loop, sometimes called a repeat until loop, keeps repeating until a certain condition becomes true, which is useful when we do not know in advance exactly how many times the loop needs to run. For example, repeat until the player reaches the finish line will keep looping for as long as needed, whether that takes five steps or fifty. It is also possible to nest loops, which means putting one loop inside another loop, useful for tasks like drawing a grid of squares, where an outer loop controls the rows and an inner loop controls the columns within each row. Choosing the right type of loop makes a program more efficient and easier to understand, and helps avoid problems such as infinite loops, where a loop never stops because its condition can never become true, which can cause a program to freeze.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Variables and selection become much more powerful when they are used together, because a program can check the value stored in a variable and then decide what to do based on that value. For example, imagine a program with a variable called lives, which starts at 3. Every time the player is hit, the program might subtract 1 from lives, and then use a selection block to check if lives is equal to 0. If this condition is true, the program can display game over, but if it is false, the game simply carries on as normal. This combination of variables and selection lets programs make sensible decisions that change depending on what has happened while the program is running, rather than always doing exactly the same thing. We can also use comparison operators to build conditions, such as checking if a variable is equal to, greater than, or less than a certain number, for example if score is greater than or equal to 100, then say you reached the high score. Combining variables and selection is one of the most useful skills in programming, because it allows programs, especially games, to respond intelligently to changing information, such as scores, lives, time remaining, or a player's choices.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using different shapes connected by arrows, making it easier to plan and understand a program before writing any code. Each shape in a flowchart has a specific meaning. An oval shape usually shows the start or end of the algorithm. A rectangle shows a step or an instruction to be carried out, such as add 1 to score. A diamond shape shows a decision, which is a question with a yes or no, or true or false, answer, matching the idea of selection that we have already learned. Arrows connect the shapes and show the order in which the steps should happen, and when a diamond decision is used, two arrows usually lead out of it, one for each possible answer, showing the different paths the algorithm could take. Flowcharts are especially useful for planning algorithms that include selection or loops, because they let us see the different possible paths through the algorithm clearly, before we try to build it using code. For example, a flowchart for checking if a password is correct might show a decision diamond asking is the password correct, with one path leading to allow access, and another path leading back to try again. Drawing a flowchart before coding helps us spot missing steps or confusing logic early on.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Debugging Strategies: Finding Logic Errors
tasks.content: As programs become more complex, using variables, selection, and loops together, bugs can become trickier to find, especially a type of bug called a logic error. A logic error happens when a program runs without crashing or showing an obvious error message, but it still produces the wrong result, because the instructions do not do quite what we intended. Logic errors can be some of the hardest bugs to find, precisely because the program appears to be working. One useful debugging strategy is called tracing, where we go through the program step by step, exactly as the computer would, writing down the value of each variable as it changes, to see exactly where the result starts to go wrong. Another useful strategy is to test the program with different inputs, including unusual or extreme ones, because a bug might only appear in certain situations, such as when a variable reaches exactly zero. It also helps to check conditions very carefully, because a small mistake, such as using greater than instead of greater than or equal to, can completely change how a selection block behaves. Reading code aloud, or explaining it to someone else line by line, often helps us notice mistakes that we have been reading past without seeing. Careful, patient, methodical debugging is what separates confusing, broken programs from clear, reliable ones.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Simulating Physical Systems with Code
tasks.content: Programs can be used to simulate, or imitate, how things behave in the real world, which is a powerful use of computing in science, engineering, and games. A simulation uses code, including variables, selection, and loops, to model a real system and show how it might change over time. For example, we could simulate a bouncing ball using a variable for its height, and a loop that repeatedly reduces the height slightly to show it falling, then uses selection to check if the ball has reached the ground, and if so, makes it bounce back upward instead of continuing to fall. Another example is simulating a simple traffic light system, using a sequence and a loop to make a light cycle through red, then red and amber together, then green, then amber, before repeating the whole sequence again, matching how real traffic lights behave. Simulations are useful because they let us explore how a system works, test out different situations safely, and predict what might happen, without needing the real physical object, which can sometimes be expensive, dangerous, or simply impossible to test directly, such as simulating weather patterns or the orbit of planets. Building a simple simulation combines everything we have learned about sequence, selection, loops, and variables into one program that models something real.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Data and Information: Collecting and Presenting

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Data and Information: Collecting and Presenting
tasks.content: Data means raw facts and figures, such as numbers or short pieces of text, which by themselves may not tell us very much. Information is what we get once data has been organised, processed, or explained in a way that makes it meaningful and useful. For example, a single number like 24 is just data, but if we say the temperature today is 24 degrees Celsius, that number has become useful information. In computing, we often collect data using tools such as questionnaires, tally charts, or sensors that automatically measure things like temperature or light levels. Once data has been collected, it usually needs to be organised, for example by entering it into a spreadsheet, sorting it into categories, or counting how often something appears. After data has been organised, we can present it clearly using tables, charts, or graphs, which often make patterns and comparisons much easier to see than looking at a long list of raw numbers. For example, a bar chart can quickly show which class had the most pupils walk to school, something that might be hard to notice by reading a plain list. Choosing the right way to present data, and making sure charts have clear titles and labels, helps other people understand our information quickly and accurately.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A database is an organised collection of information, stored on a computer, so that it can be easily searched, sorted, and updated. Databases are usually organised into tables, which look similar to a spreadsheet, made up of rows and columns. Each row in a table is called a record, and represents one complete set of information about a single thing, such as one pupil, one book, or one product. Each column is called a field, and represents one particular piece of information collected about every record, such as name, age, or favourite colour. For example, a simple school library database might have a table where each record is one book, and the fields include title, author, and whether the book is currently available to borrow. One of the most useful things about a database is that we can search it, using specific criteria, to quickly find matching records, for example searching for every book written by a particular author, without needing to look through a long list by hand. We can also sort a database, for example putting all the books in order by title or by author's surname, and we can filter it, showing only the records that match certain conditions, such as only books that are currently available. Databases are used constantly in real life, including school registers, library systems, medical records, and online shops.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: How Search Engines Rank Results
tasks.content: When we search for something online, a search engine does not simply show us every website that mentions our search words in a random order. Instead, it uses a set of rules and calculations, called an algorithm, to work out which results are most likely to be useful, and shows the results ranked with the most relevant ones near the top of the list. Search engines look at many different clues to decide how to rank a webpage. One important clue is relevance, which means how closely the words and content on a page match what we searched for. Another important clue is how trustworthy or popular a website seems to be, which search engines can partly judge by how many other reliable websites link to it, a bit like how a well-recommended shop might be trusted more than one nobody has ever mentioned. Search engines also consider how well a website works, such as whether it loads quickly and works properly on a phone or tablet, not just a computer. Because search engines use algorithms to rank results, and because some website owners try hard to appear near the top of search results, it is still important to think carefully about the results we click on, and remember that being ranked first does not automatically mean a website is completely accurate or trustworthy, only that a search engine's algorithm judged it as likely to be relevant and useful.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Online Safety: Cyberbullying and Reporting
tasks.content: Cyberbullying means using technology, such as messaging apps, games, or social media, to deliberately upset, embarrass, threaten, or be unkind to someone, repeatedly and on purpose. It can include sending unkind or threatening messages, spreading untrue or hurtful rumours online, deliberately leaving someone out of online groups or games, or sharing embarrassing pictures or videos of someone without their permission. Cyberbullying can feel especially difficult because it can follow a person outside of school, sometimes even into their own home, and hurtful messages can be seen again and again, or shared further to other people. It is important to remember that cyberbullying is never the fault of the person experiencing it, and nobody deserves to be treated that way. If cyberbullying happens to you, or you see it happening to somebody else, the most important step is to tell a trusted adult, such as a parent, carer, or teacher, straight away, rather than dealing with it alone or in secret. Most apps, games, and websites also have a reporting or blocking feature, which allows us to report unkind behaviour to the people who run the website, and to block a person so they can no longer contact us. Keeping evidence, such as not deleting a hurtful message straight away, can also help a trusted adult understand exactly what happened and how to help.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Creating a multimedia presentation means combining several types of media, such as text, images, sound, and sometimes video, into a single organised project that explains an idea clearly to an audience. Before creating slides, it helps to plan the whole presentation first, deciding on the overall purpose, the main points to be covered, and a sensible order for those points, so that the presentation flows logically from beginning to end. Each slide should usually focus on just one main idea, with a short, clear heading, and only as much text as is needed, because slides that are too crowded with writing can be hard for an audience to read and follow. Images should be chosen carefully to support and illustrate the point being made on that slide, rather than being added just to fill space, and any sound or narration should be clear and add real value, rather than distracting from the message. It is also important to check that the presentation is consistent, using similar fonts, colours, and layouts throughout, so it looks professional and organised rather than messy. Once the presentation is finished, it is worth practising going through it, checking that everything works correctly, that the information is accurate, and that the order of slides makes logical sense, before sharing it with an audience.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every sprite in Scratch can have more than one costume, which are different pictures or poses that make up how the sprite looks. Think of costumes like frames in a flip book: each one is slightly different, and when you flip through them quickly, one after another, it creates the illusion of movement, even though each costume is really just a still picture. This is exactly how sprite animation works in Scratch! For example, a walking cat sprite might have two costumes, one with its legs together, and one with its legs apart, mid-step. If we switch back and forth between these two costumes quickly, using the "next costume" block inside a loop, combined with a small "wait" block between each switch, the cat will appear to actually be walking, even though we are just swapping between two simple pictures over and over. The "next costume" block automatically moves to the very next costume in the sprite's costume list, and after the last costume, it loops back around to the first one again. We can also switch directly to a specific costume by name, using the "switch costume to" block, which is useful for showing an exact pose at an exact moment, like switching to a "surprised" costume the instant a sprite touches something unexpected. Good animation usually combines costume changes with motion blocks at the same time, so a character is not just changing its look, but also actually traveling across the stage, just like the walking cat example. The timing of the "wait" block matters quite a lot too: too short a wait and the animation looks like a blur, too long a wait and it looks jerky and slow instead of smooth. Today we will look at a sprite's costume list, build a walking or flying animation using "next costume" inside a loop, and adjust our wait times until the motion looks smooth and natural.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: So far, each sprite's code has mostly worked on its own, but what if we want one sprite's actions to affect a completely different sprite? That is exactly what broadcasting is for! Broadcasting lets one sprite send a message that any other sprite in the project can listen for and react to, even though the sprites are not directly connected to each other in any other way. To use broadcasting, we use two special event blocks: "broadcast message," which sends out a chosen message to the entire project, and "when I receive message," which starts a script on any sprite that is listening for that exact same message. For example, imagine a game where a wizard sprite casts a spell, and we want a dragon sprite, somewhere else in the project, to disappear the moment the spell is cast. We could give the wizard sprite a script that broadcasts a message called "spell cast" the moment the spell button is pressed. Then, on the dragon sprite, we would build a separate script that starts with "when I receive spell cast," followed by a "hide" block, making the dragon disappear at exactly the right moment. Notice that the wizard sprite does not need to know anything at all about the dragon sprite, it just broadcasts the message out into the whole project, and any sprite that cares can react however it wants to. This makes broadcasting incredibly powerful for coordinating many sprites at once, like starting a whole scene change, or signaling that a level is complete, without needing to write complicated code connecting every single sprite directly to every other sprite. Today we will build a two-sprite project where one sprite broadcasts a message and a second sprite reacts to it, testing what happens when the message is sent at different times.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In Grade 2, we had a first, simple look at loops within loops. Now, as our Scratch projects grow more advanced, let's dive deeper into nested loops, loops placed inside other loops, and see how powerful they can be for creating patterns and repeated behaviors. When we nest a loop inside another loop, the inner loop must completely finish all of its repeats before the outer loop can continue on to its next repeat. Let's look at a drawing example using the pen blocks in Scratch: imagine we want to draw a grid of dots, three rows of dots, with five dots in each row. We could use an outer loop that says "repeat 3," for the three rows, and inside it, an inner loop that says "repeat 5," for the five dots in each row, with a "stamp" block and a "move" block inside the inner loop to actually draw each dot and move over slightly before drawing the next one. After the inner loop finishes drawing all five dots in a row, the outer loop would move the pen down to the next row, and then the inner loop would run again, drawing five more dots. In total, this nested loop would draw fifteen dots, three rows multiplied by five dots each. Nested loops are also extremely useful for animations, like a sprite that needs to blink twice, every time it takes a step, for several steps in a row, in which case the blinking would be the inner loop, and the stepping would be the outer loop. When working with nested loops, it helps to think about which action is the "big" repeating action, which becomes the outer loop, and which action is the "small" repeating action that happens inside each big repeat, which becomes the inner loop. Today we will use nested loops with pen blocks to draw a simple repeated shape pattern, calculating ahead of time exactly how many total shapes our nested loops should create.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In Grade 3, we learned about the if-then block, which runs certain blocks only when a condition is true, and skips them otherwise. This year, we are learning about its more powerful cousin: the if-else block! An if-else block still checks whether a condition is true or false, but now it has two separate sets of blocks: one set that runs if the condition is true, and a completely different set that runs if the condition is false, instead of simply being skipped. This means an if-else block always runs something, either the "if" part or the "else" part, never both, and never neither. Let's think of an example: a quiz game sprite that checks whether a player clicked the correct answer. Using if-else, we could write: "if answer is correct, then say Great job! and change score by 1, else say Try again! and change lives by negative 1." Notice how both outcomes, getting it right and getting it wrong, are handled within a single block, instead of needing two completely separate if-then blocks checking opposite conditions. This makes our code shorter, clearer, and much less likely to have mistakes, since we do not have to remember to write a second, opposite condition ourselves. If-else blocks are perfect anytime there are exactly two possible outcomes: win or lose, open or closed, day or night, touching or not touching. When there might be three or more possible outcomes, coders often use several if-else blocks together, or a similar block called "if-else if," which we may explore in later grades. Today we will convert a project that uses two separate if-then blocks into a single, cleaner if-else block, and we will build a new script from scratch using if-else to handle a true and false outcome differently.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Operators: Math and Comparison Blocks
tasks.content: Operator blocks in Scratch are green, and they let our programs do math and make comparisons, which is especially useful when combined with variables and if-else blocks. Math operator blocks include addition, like "__ + __", subtraction, like "__ - __", multiplication, and division, letting our programs calculate numbers while the project is running, instead of us calculating everything by hand ahead of time. Comparison operator blocks, on the other hand, compare two values and return either true or false, which makes them perfect for fitting inside the hexagon-shaped condition slot of an if-then or if-else block. The three main comparison operators are greater than, shown as "__ > __", less than, shown as "__ < __", and equal to, shown as "__ = __". For example, imagine a game where a player wins once their score reaches 10 points. We could use an if-then block with the condition "score > 9", or equally correctly, "score = 10", to check whether the player has reached the winning score, and then show a "You win!" message once that condition becomes true. Operators can also be combined with each other, like using multiplication inside an addition block, letting us build more complex math expressions out of simple building blocks, the same way we snap together motion or sound blocks. There are also operators for combining true and false conditions, like "and", "or", and "not", which let us check multiple conditions at the same time, such as "if score > 9 and lives > 0", which would only be true if both parts are true at the very same time. Today we will practice building simple math expressions with operator blocks, and we will use comparison operators inside if-then and if-else blocks to check score and lives conditions in a sample project.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Using Variables for Score and Lives

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Using Variables for Score and Lives
tasks.content: We first learned about variables in Grade 3, using them to keep score. This year, we will go further, using multiple variables together, like score and lives, to build more complete and realistic games. Just like score, a lives variable stores a number, usually starting at a value like 3, representing how many chances a player has before the game ends. As the game runs, we use "change lives by -1" whenever the player makes a mistake, like a sprite getting hit by an obstacle, and we use an if-then block to check whether lives has reached 0, which would trigger the game to end. Combining score and lives together creates much more interesting games than using either variable alone. For example, imagine a game where a player collects coins to increase their score, but loses a life every time they touch a spike. We would need an if-then block checking "touching coin" that leads to "change score by 1", and a separate if-then block checking "touching spike" that leads to "change lives by -1", and then another if-then block checking "lives = 0" that leads to broadcasting a "game over" message. Because variables can be shown on the stage, players can watch both their score and their remaining lives update in real time as they play, which makes the game feel exciting and keeps players motivated to keep trying. It is also important to reset variables back to their starting values, like setting score to 0 and lives to 3, using "set" blocks connected to the green flag event, so that every new game starts fresh instead of continuing from the numbers left over by the last time the game was played. Today we will build a small game using both a score variable and a lives variable together, making sure both reset correctly at the start of a new game.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A variable can only hold one piece of information at a time, like a single score number. But what if we need to remember many pieces of information at once, like a list of high scores, or the names of several players? That is exactly what a list is for! A list is like a variable, but instead of one box, it is a whole row of numbered boxes, each one able to hold its own separate piece of information. In Scratch, lists appear alongside variables, shown as an orange block category, and they can be shown on the stage just like variables can, displaying every item in the list at once. To use a list, we first create it and give it a name, like "high scores." Then we can use blocks like "add __ to list," which adds a new item to the very end of the list, "delete __ of list," which removes an item at a specific position, and "item __ of list," which lets us look up and use whatever is stored at a specific position in the list. For example, imagine a game that keeps track of the five most recent scores from different rounds played. Every time a round ends, we could use "add score to high scores," adding the newest score to the end of the list, building up a growing record over time. We could also use a loop combined with "item __ of list" to display every single score stored in the list, one at a time, perhaps showing them as a scrolling record of past attempts. Lists are incredibly useful anytime a program needs to keep track of more than one piece of information, like a shopping list, a set of player names, or a collection of words for a spelling game. Today we will create a list, add several items to it using blocks, and use a loop to display every item stored inside it.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: As our projects use more and more variables, like score, lives, and lists, a new and very useful debugging skill becomes important: using variables themselves to help us find bugs! One of the best debugging tricks in Scratch is to show a variable on the stage while testing a project, watching its value change in real time as the project runs, instead of guessing whether it is working correctly. For example, if a score variable is not increasing the way we expect when a sprite touches a coin, we can show the score variable on the stage and watch closely: does it increase at all? Does it increase by the wrong amount, like 2 instead of 1? Does it increase at the wrong time, like when touching the wrong sprite instead of the coin? Watching the variable update, or fail to update, gives us important clues about exactly where the mistake might be hiding. Another useful trick is creating a temporary "debug" variable specifically to track information while we are testing, even if we plan to remove it later, once everything works correctly. For example, we might create a variable called "debug" and set it to show which if-then block condition most recently became true, helping us understand the order that different parts of our code are actually running in, which is not always obvious just by reading the blocks. We can also use lists for debugging, adding a short message to a list every time an important event happens in our code, building up a kind of history log we can look back through afterward to see exactly what happened, and in what order. Today we will intentionally break a working project by changing one variable-related block, and we will use variable-watching techniques to find and fix the mistake.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Building a Maze or Chase Game

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Building a Maze or Chase Game
tasks.content: Now let's combine everything we have learned this year, costumes and animation, broadcasting, nested loops, if-else blocks, operators, variables for score and lives, and lists, into one exciting final type of project: a maze or chase game! In a maze game, a sprite must navigate through a path filled with walls, using arrow key events and motion blocks, while an if-then block continuously checks whether the sprite is touching a wall color, sending it back to the start if it bumps into one. In a chase game, instead of walls, one sprite, like a player-controlled character, is chased by another sprite, controlled by code instead of a player, using motion blocks combined with a loop that constantly points and moves the chaser toward the player's position. Building a full maze or chase game requires planning: first, sketch the maze layout or the chase area on paper. Second, decide exactly how the player will control their sprite, usually with arrow key events. Third, decide what makes the player win, like reaching a goal spot in a maze, and what makes the player lose, like running out of lives after being caught by a chaser. Fourth, decide where variables are needed, like a lives variable that decreases each time the chaser catches the player, or a timer that counts down. As we build, we will use if-else blocks to handle two-way outcomes, like whether the player reached the goal or not, operators to compare positions or scores, and broadcasting to signal important moments, like starting a new level or ending the game. This project brings together nearly every single coding concept we have learned since Grade 1, from simple sequencing all the way up to lists and operators. Today we will begin planning and building our own maze or chase game, working through each planning question before opening Scratch to start building.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: You have reached the end of an amazing year of coding, and your skills have grown enormously! This year, you learned to animate sprites using costumes, send broadcast messages between sprites, build nested loops for complex repeating patterns, make two-way decisions with if-else blocks, use operator blocks for math and comparisons, track score and lives with variables, store multiple pieces of information using lists, debug using variables and history logs, and even design a full maze or chase game. For your final mini project of the year, you will design and build a complete Scratch project that shows off as many of these skills as possible, working almost entirely on your own, just like a real programmer. Begin, as always, with planning: What is your project about? What sprites, costumes, and backgrounds will you need? What events will control the action? Where will you need loops, if-then or if-else blocks, variables, or even a list? Sketch your plan on paper before opening Scratch, listing out the blocks and concepts you expect to use. As you build, work in small, testable pieces, just like we have practiced all year, checking that each part works correctly before adding the next one. Use your debugging skills whenever something does not behave the way you expect, watching your variables, checking your event blocks, and looking closely at your if-then and if-else conditions. When your project is complete, take time to test it thoroughly, trying to "break" it on purpose by doing unexpected things, like clicking sprites in a strange order, to make sure it still behaves correctly. Finally, share your finished project with classmates, and take time to explore theirs as well, noticing the different, creative ways everyone combined the very same coding tools. You have built a strong foundation in coding this year, and you are ready to take on even bigger and more exciting challenges in the future. Great work, coder!
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Summarising means capturing a text's key points in far fewer words than the original, using your own phrasing rather than copying sentences. A strong summary keeps the main ideas and cuts repetition, examples and minor detail. Critical analysis goes further: it asks whether the writer's argument is convincing, what evidence they use, and whether their viewpoint might be biased or one-sided. Skilled readers separate what a text says (fact) from what it wants you to think (opinion).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In the active voice, the subject of the sentence performs the action, as in 'The dog chased the ball.' In the passive voice, the subject receives the action instead, as in 'The ball was chased by the dog,' formed with a form of 'to be' plus a past participle. Writers choose the passive voice to focus attention on the action or the receiver rather than who did it, or when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The window was broken.' Recognising both forms helps you control emphasis and formality in your own writing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The subjunctive mood is used for hypothetical, wished-for or formal situations, such as 'If I were you, I would apologise' or 'The teacher insisted that he arrive on time.' Notice that the verb form often differs from ordinary agreement, for example using 'were' instead of 'was' for all subjects, or the base form of the verb after words like 'suggest,' 'demand' or 'insist.' The subjunctive is common in formal or written English and signals that something is imagined, wished for, or required rather than a plain fact.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Cohesion is what makes a piece of writing flow as one connected whole rather than a list of separate sentences. Writers achieve this using adverbials (such as 'meanwhile,' 'as a result,' 'later that day') to link ideas across paragraphs, pronouns to avoid repeating nouns, and deliberate repetition or synonyms to keep a reader tracking the same idea. Strong cohesion guides the reader smoothly from one point to the next without confusing jumps.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A colon introduces a list, an explanation or an example, as in 'She packed three things: a map, a torch and water.' A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, as in 'The rain stopped; the sun came out,' or separates items in a complex list. A hyphen joins words to form a compound, such as 'well-known' or 'long-term,' and can prevent ambiguity, as in 're-cover' versus 'recover.' Choosing the right mark makes your meaning precise.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Extended narrative writing means planning and sustaining a story across multiple paragraphs or chapters rather than a single short scene. Strong long-form stories need a clear structure — an opening that establishes character and setting, rising action with complications, a climax, and a resolution — plus consistent characters and a controlled pace. Planning a story arc before you write helps you avoid rushing the ending or losing track of subplots, and revisiting earlier details, like a promise or an object, later in the story builds satisfying cohesion.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Journalistic writing reports events in a clear, factual style while sometimes including opinion in clearly labelled sections such as comment or editorial pieces. News reports typically open with a headline and a strong first paragraph answering who, what, when, where and why, then add supporting facts, quotations and details in order of importance — a structure called the 'inverted pyramid.' Good journalism keeps fact and opinion clearly separate, uses quotations to add authority, and writes in a tone suited to its audience.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This unit reviews the statutory Year 6 grammar and punctuation requirements: using the passive and subjunctive appropriately, punctuating bullet points and speech correctly, and using semicolons, colons and dashes to signal a range of relationships between clauses. It also revises expanded noun phrases, relative clauses, and the correct use of commas to clarify meaning, such as separating a subordinate clause from the main clause. Confident, accurate use of these features across a whole piece of writing is expected by the end of primary school.

tasks.content: Poets choose form (the shape and structure of a poem, such as its stanza pattern, line length or rhyme scheme) and imagery (descriptive language that appeals to the senses, including metaphor and simile) to create effect and meaning beyond the literal words. A short, fragmented line might mirror a character's breathlessness or shock, while a regular rhythm can suggest calm or inevitability. When analysing a poem, ask not just what an image means but why the poet placed it exactly where they did, and what that structural choice adds to the poem's meaning.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Effective spoken argument requires a clear structure: state your point, support it with evidence or reasoning, and address opposing views before summarising. Good debaters adapt their tone, pace and vocabulary to their audience, use rhetorical techniques such as rhetorical questions and the rule of three to persuade, and listen actively so they can respond to counter-arguments rather than simply repeating prepared points. Preparing key points in advance, along with anticipated objections, builds confidence for formal spoken argument.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every digit in a large number has a value based on its column: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions, and ten millions. In 6,428,571 the 6 is worth 6,000,000, the 4 is worth 400,000, and so on, so we can partition it as 6,000,000 + 400,000 + 20,000 + 8,000 + 500 + 70 + 1. To round a number, look at the digit to the right of the column you are rounding to: 6,482,913 rounded to the nearest 100,000 is 6,500,000, because the ten-thousands digit (8) rounds up.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Formal written methods let us add, subtract, multiply and divide large numbers accurately. For addition and subtraction, line up the columns and carry or borrow as needed: 3,847 + 2,956 = 6,803. For short division, divide each digit in turn and carry remainders: 4,236 divided by 6 is 706, because 6 x 706 = 4,236. Practising these methods with a range of numbers builds the speed and accuracy you need for harder problems.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways of showing the same value, and we can convert between them. To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator; to change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100. For example, 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. To simplify a decimal into a fraction, write it over 100 (or 1000) and cancel down: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

tasks.content: A ratio compares two or more quantities and can be simplified like a fraction by dividing by the highest common factor. To share an amount in a given ratio, add the parts to find the total number of parts, divide the amount by this total to find the value of one part, then multiply. For example, to share £24 in the ratio 3:5, there are 8 parts in total, so each part is £3, giving shares of £9 and £15.

tasks.content: Metric units scale by powers of 10: 1km = 1000m, 1m = 100cm, 1kg = 1000g, and 1 litre = 1000ml. Imperial units are still used in everyday life alongside them, and rough conversions are useful: 1 mile is approximately 1.6km, and 1kg is approximately 2.2 pounds. For example, to convert 4.2km to metres, multiply by 1000 to get 4,200m; to convert 5 miles to kilometres, multiply by 1.6 to get about 8km.

tasks.content: A compound shape is made of two or more basic shapes joined together, so to find its area, split it into rectangles or triangles, find each area separately, then add (or subtract, if a piece has been removed) them. Perimeter is the total distance around the outside, found by adding every outer side length. For example, an L-shape made from a 6cm by 4cm rectangle and a 3cm by 2cm rectangle has a total area of 24 + 6 = 30cm².
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: 2D shapes can be classified by their sides and angles: a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides, a parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides with no right angles required, and a rhombus has four equal sides but is not always a square. Triangles are classified by their sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) or angles (acute, right-angled, obtuse). 3D shapes are described by their faces, edges and vertices: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

tasks.content: Living things are sorted into groups based on shared characteristics, a process called classification. Scientists use a hierarchy including kingdoms such as animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms, and within animals further groups like vertebrates and invertebrates. Classification keys, such as branching (dichotomous) keys, ask yes/no questions to help identify an unknown organism. Grouping living things this way helps scientists communicate clearly and spot patterns in how organisms are related.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Inheritance is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring through genetic information. Offspring resemble their parents but are not identical to them or to each other, because of variation. Evolution is the gradual change in species over many generations, driven by natural selection: organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those characteristics on. Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explains how today's wide variety of species developed from earlier life forms over millions of years.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The circulatory system moves blood around the body, carrying oxygen and nutrients to cells and removing waste products like carbon dioxide. The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers that pushes blood through a network of blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry blood back to the heart, and tiny capillaries connect them and allow exchange of substances with body tissues. Blood itself contains red blood cells, which carry oxygen using a substance called haemoglobin, as well as white blood cells that fight infection and plasma that carries dissolved substances.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A healthy, balanced diet provides the right nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water) in the correct amounts for the body's needs, which vary with age, activity level and health. Regular exercise keeps the heart and muscles strong and helps maintain a healthy body weight, while too little exercise or an unbalanced diet can lead to health problems such as obesity or malnutrition. Drugs, including legal ones like alcohol, tobacco and caffeine, change how the body functions and can harm health, particularly the heart, lungs and liver, which is why understanding their effects on lifestyle is important.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: We see objects because light travels from a light source, bounces (reflects) off objects, and enters our eyes. Light enters through the transparent cornea and pupil, and the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye, where light-sensitive cells detect it. The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to the brain, where the image is interpreted. Light travels in straight lines, which is why we can only see an object if there is a straight, unblocked path from it to our eyes.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to show how components are connected in an electrical circuit, making it easy for anyone to read and build the same circuit. Common symbols include a straight line for a wire, a circle with a line through it for a cell (battery), a circle with a cross for a bulb, a zigzag or rectangle for a resistor, and a break in a line with a lever for a switch. In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop one after another, so if one component is removed or breaks, the whole circuit stops working.

tasks.content: Adaptations are special features or behaviours that help a living thing survive and reproduce in its particular habitat. Structural adaptations are physical features, such as a polar bear's thick fur and fat for warmth in the Arctic, or a cactus's spines and thick stem for storing water in the desert. Behavioural adaptations are things an animal does, such as migrating to warmer places or hibernating through winter to save energy. Over many generations, species become well suited to their environment through natural selection, but if their habitat changes too quickly they may struggle to survive.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A full scientific investigation starts with a clear question and a prediction of what you expect to happen and why. You then plan a fair test by identifying the independent variable (the one thing you change), the dependent variable (what you measure), and the control variables (everything kept the same), along with choosing suitable equipment and repeating measurements for reliability. After carrying out the investigation safely, results are recorded in a table, often displayed in a graph, and then used to draw a conclusion that answers the original question, explaining whether the prediction was correct.
Let's practice what we just learned!

This often involves reading a short passage or looking at results, then answering questions that ask you to identify patterns, make comparisons, or explain why something happened using the correct scientific vocabulary. Practising these skills, similar to those used in KS2 SATs, helps you show not just what you know, but how well you can think and reason like a scientist.

tasks.content: Tamil nouns change their ending, called a vetrumai urubu (வேற்றுமை உருபு), to show their role in a sentence, similar to how English uses word order or prepositions. For example, adding கு (ku) makes a noun a dative case, as in "அவனுக்கு" (avanukku, "to/for him"), while adding ஆல் (aal) makes it instrumental, as in "கையால்" (kaiyaal, "by hand"). Traditional Tamil grammar names eight cases in order: எழுவாய் (nominative), செயப்படுபொருள் (accusative, -ஐ), கருவி (instrumental, -ஆல்), கொடை (dative, -கு), நீங்கல் (ablative, -இல் இருந்து), உடைமை (genitive, -இன்), இடம் (locative, -இல்/கண்) and விளி (vocative). Learning these urubus lets you build precise sentences like "நான் பேனையால் எழுதுகிறேன்" (I write with a pen).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Tamil has two important non-finite verb forms that let you link actions or describe nouns without a full separate sentence. A vinaiyechcham (வினையெச்சம், adverbial participle) shows one action happening before another, like "சாப்பிட்டு படுத்தான்" (saapittu paduthaan, "having eaten, he lay down"), formed by adding -டு/-து to a verb stem. A peyarechcham (பெயரெச்சம், relative/adjectival participle) turns a verb into a word that describes a noun, like "படித்த மாணவன்" (padittha maanavan, "the student who studied", past tense) or "படிக்கும் மாணவன்" (the student who will study/studies, future/habitual). Notice how the peyarechcham always comes directly before the noun it describes, unlike English relative clauses that use "who" or "which".
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The Thirukkural (திருக்குறள்) is a classic Tamil work of 1,330 rhyming couplets (குறள்), traditionally attributed to the poet Thiruvalluvar (திருவள்ளுவர்) and composed roughly 2,000 years ago. It is organised into three major sections called pal (பால்): அறம் (Aram, virtue/ethics, 380 couplets), பொருள் (Porul, wealth and governance) and இன்பம் (Inbam, love). Aram Pal opens with a chapter praising God (கடவுள் வாழ்த்து), and its very first couplet begins "அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம்" (agara mudhala ezhuthellaam), meaning that just as the letter அ (a) is the first of all letters, the eternal one is first in the world. Aram Pal goes on to teach virtues such as honesty, gratitude and kindness for everyday life.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Tamil Kings: The Chola, Pandya & Chera Dynasties
tasks.content: Long ago, ancient Tamil land (Tamilakam) was ruled by three great royal families, often called மூவேந்தர் (the "Three Crowned Kings"): the சோழர் (Chola), பாண்டியர் (Pandya), and சேரர் (Chera). Each dynasty ruled a different region and had its own symbol (emblem). The Cholas ruled the fertile Kaveri river valley in the east, and their emblem was the tiger. Their early capital was Uraiyur. The Pandyas ruled the south, with their capital at மதுரை (Madurai), and their emblem was the fish (carp). Madurai was also a great center of learning, home to the Tamil Sangams — academies of poets who composed and preserved classical Tamil literature. The Cheras ruled the west, in what is now Kerala, with their capital near Vanji, and their emblem was the bow. These three kingdoms sometimes fought each other for power, but they also supported poets, temples, and trade, and their courts are where much of the earliest Tamil literature, called Sangam literature, was composed and collected.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Sangam literature (சங்க இலக்கியம், Sangam Ilakkiyam) is the oldest surviving body of Tamil poetry, traditionally linked to gatherings of poets called sangams said to have met under royal patronage in Madurai. Scholars generally date the surviving poems to roughly the last centuries BCE through the early centuries CE, making it one of the most ancient literatures in India. The poems are organised into two great collections: எட்டுத்தொகை (Ettuthogai, the "Eight Anthologies") and பத்துப்பாட்டு (Pathuppaattu, the "Ten Idylls" or "Ten Songs"). Sangam poetry is traditionally divided by theme into அகம் (agam, poems about inner/personal life such as love) and புறம் (puram, poems about outer/public life such as war, kingship and heroism).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A formal Tamil letter (முறையான கடிதம், muraiyaana kadidham) follows a set structure: it opens with the sender's முகவரி (address) and தேதி (date), followed by a respectful salutation such as "அன்புள்ள ஐயா/அம்மா" (Dear Sir/Madam). The body states its purpose clearly and politely — for example, requesting leave from school might begin "தாழ்மையுடன் தெரிவிப்பது என்னவெனில்" (I humbly wish to inform you that...). It closes with a polite sign-off such as "இங்ஙனம்" (yours truly) or "தங்கள் உண்மையுள்ள" followed by கையொப்பம் (signature) and பெயர் (name). Keeping a formal, respectful tone throughout — avoiding casual spoken-Tamil words — is essential in this kind of writing.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Growing your Tamil vocabulary means learning ஒப்புச்சொல் (oppuchchol, synonyms), எதிர்ச்சொல் (edhirchol, antonyms), and வேர்ச்சொல் (verchol, root words) that connect whole families of related words. For example, "மகிழ்ச்சி" (magizhchi, happiness) shares its meaning with "சந்தோஷம்" (santhosham) — both are synonyms for joy. Antonym pairs include "நல்லது" (good) and "கெட்டது" (bad), or "பெரியது" (big) and "சிறியது" (small). A single root like "படி" (padi, to study/read) grows into a whole word family: "படிப்பு" (padippu, education/study, noun), "படித்தல்" (padithal, the act of reading) and "படிப்பாளி" (padippaali, a scholar) — noticing these shared roots helps you guess the meaning of new words.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A Tamil essay, கட்டுரை (kattturai), follows a clear three-part shape that keeps your ideas organised for the reader. It opens with a முன்னுரை (munnurai, introduction) that presents the topic, moves into a வளர்ச்சி (valarchi, body/development) where you build several paragraphs of supporting ideas and examples, and ends with a முடிவுரை (mudivurai, conclusion) that sums up your main point. For example, an essay titled "சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு" (environmental protection) might introduce why the environment matters, develop paragraphs on pollution and solutions, then conclude with a call to action. Planning these three parts before you begin writing helps you stay focused and avoid repeating yourself.
Let's practice what we just learned!
