. Links, which let visitors click to jump to another page or website, use the tag, short for "anchor." Unlike headings and paragraphs, a link tag needs an extra piece of information called an attribute, specifically href (short for "hypertext reference"), which tells the browser where the link should go. A working link looks like this: Visit Wikipedia. Here, "Visit Wikipedia" is the clickable text the visitor sees, while the href attribute, placed inside the opening tag and set in quotation marks, is the actual web address the browser navigates to when clicked. You can combine all of these on one page: an

title, a couple of

section headings, several

paragraphs explaining each section, and links pointing to related pages, and this combination, using the right tag for the right kind of content, is exactly what makes a web page organized and easy to navigate. Getting comfortable choosing the correct tag, a heading for titles, a paragraph for text, a link for navigation, is one of the most important habits in HTML, because search engines and screen readers for visually impaired users rely on this structure to understand your page correctly.

levels.levelName: Introduction to CSS: Styling Text and Color

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Introduction to CSS: Styling Text and Color
tasks.content:
If HTML is the skeleton of a web page, CSS, which stands for Cascading Style Sheets, is what gives it color, fonts, spacing, and visual style. Without CSS, every web page would look like plain black text on a white background, with no design at all. CSS works by writing "rules" that select which HTML elements to style and then describe what properties to change. A CSS rule has three parts: a selector, which says which HTML tag or element to target; curly braces, which contain the styling instructions; and inside those braces, property-value pairs separated by colons and ending in semicolons. For example, this rule makes every paragraph's text blue and slightly larger: p { color: blue; font-size: 18px; }. Here, "p" is the selector targeting all

tags, "color" and "font-size" are properties, and "blue" and "18px" are their values. CSS can be added to an HTML page in a few ways, but a common beginner-friendly method is placing a . This would make every

heading red and every paragraph green throughout the page. You can style many properties: color changes text color, background-color changes the background behind an element, font-size changes text size, and font-family changes which typeface is used, like Arial or Georgia. A key idea behind CSS's name is "cascading," meaning styles can flow down and combine from multiple rules, and more specific rules generally override more general ones. Learning to separate structure, handled by HTML, from style, handled by CSS, is one of the most important ideas in web development, because it lets you completely redesign how a page looks, colors, fonts, layout, without ever having to change the actual content or structure underneath it.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Debugging HTML and CSS Code
tasks.content:
Just like Scratch projects can have bugs, HTML and CSS code can have mistakes that stop a web page from looking or working the way you intended, and learning to debug them is an essential skill. HTML bugs are often structural: forgetting a closing tag, like writing

Hello without

, can cause everything after it to be affected unexpectedly, since the browser doesn't know where that paragraph is supposed to end. Mismatched or improperly nested tags, like writing text instead of the correctly nested text, can also cause unpredictable results, because tags must close in the reverse order they opened, like stacking and unstacking boxes. A misspelled tag name, like instead of

, simply won't be recognized by the browser at all, so it gets ignored rather than causing an error message, which can make it tricky to notice at first. CSS bugs are often about small punctuation details: forgetting a semicolon between property-value pairs, forgetting a colon between a property and its value, or misspelling a property name like "collor" instead of "color," will cause that specific style to silently fail without breaking the rest of the page. Modern web browsers include a powerful, free debugging tool called Developer Tools, usually opened by right-clicking a page and choosing "Inspect," which lets you see the actual HTML structure and CSS rules being applied, along with any errors, directly in a panel next to the page. A good debugging habit is to make one small change at a time and refresh the page to check the result, rather than changing many things at once and getting confused about which change caused which effect. It also helps to read your code out loud, tag by tag, checking that every opening tag has a matching closing tag and every CSS rule has its colon and semicolon, since these small, easy-to-miss punctuation details are the most common source of bugs in HTML and CSS.

tasks.content: You've already used flowcharts to plan Scratch games, but flowcharts are just as useful for everyday, real-world problems that have nothing to do with a screen at all. A flowchart is a visual map of decisions and steps, and once you get comfortable creating them, you'll start noticing that almost any process with choices can be turned into one. Take a simple real-world example: deciding what to wear based on the weather. Start (oval) leads to a decision diamond, "Is it raining?" If yes, an arrow leads to the action "wear a raincoat and boots." If no, the flow continues to another diamond, "Is it cold?" If yes, "wear a jacket"; if no, "wear a t-shirt." All paths then lead to an End oval. Notice how this flowchart handles every possible situation, rain, cold-but-dry, and warm-and-dry, using a chain of decision diamonds, which is exactly how programs handle multiple possible conditions using if/elif/else logic, something you'll learn directly in Python soon. Flowcharts are also incredibly useful for planning things like a morning routine, a recipe with substitutions ("if you don't have butter, use oil instead"), a school library's book checkout process, or even a chatbot's set of responses. When building a real-world flowchart, start by identifying the goal (the End oval) and the starting point (the Start oval), then ask yourself: what decisions have to be made along the way, and what happens for each possible answer? It's important that every decision diamond has an outgoing arrow for every possible answer, yes AND no, so there's never a dead end where the flowchart doesn't know what to do next. This habit of thinking through every possible branch, not just the expected one, is one of the most valuable skills in all of computer science, because real programs constantly have to handle situations the programmer didn't originally expect, like a user entering unexpected information.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Writing Pseudocode for Simple Programs
tasks.content: Building on what you learned in Grade 5, pseudocode is your plain-English planning tool, and this lesson focuses on using it for simple, real programs you're about to build for real, not just imagined Scratch projects. As you move toward Python next year, pseudocode becomes even more valuable because it lets you plan a program's logic clearly before worrying about Python's exact rules, like colons, indentation, and parentheses. Good pseudocode for a simple program uses consistent action words: INPUT for getting information from a user, SET for creating or changing a variable, IF/ELSE for decisions, and REPEAT or WHILE for loops. Let's write pseudocode for a simple program that tells someone if they can vote: START, INPUT age, IF age is greater than or equal to 18 THEN OUTPUT "You can vote!" ELSE OUTPUT "You cannot vote yet." END. Notice this pseudocode doesn't worry about Python syntax like input() or print(), it just focuses on the logic: get information, make a decision, show a result. Here's a second example, pseudocode for a program that adds up numbers a user enters until they type 0: START, SET total to 0, REPEAT: INPUT a number, IF the number equals 0 THEN STOP the repeat, ELSE add the number to total, OUTPUT total, END. This captures a loop with an exit condition, something you'll soon write as a real "while" loop in Python. When writing your own pseudocode, a helpful habit is using indentation to show which steps belong inside an IF or a REPEAT, just like nested boxes, because this visual structure maps almost exactly onto how real code is organized too. Once your pseudocode correctly handles the normal case, the age is definitely over 18, and edge cases, what if the age is exactly 18, or what if someone enters a negative age, translating it into working code in any language becomes a much smaller, more manageable step.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every single program ever written, no matter the language, whether it's Scratch, HTML, Python, or something running a spaceship, is built from just three fundamental building blocks: sequencing, selection, and iteration. Understanding these three names gives you the vocabulary to talk about ANY program's structure, and once you can spot them, code in any language starts to feel much more familiar. Sequencing simply means running instructions one after another, in order, from top to bottom, exactly as written. For example, INPUT name, then OUTPUT "Hello, " + name, then OUTPUT "Welcome!" runs as a sequence: first get the name, then greet, then welcome, always in that exact order. Selection means choosing between different paths based on a condition, using IF, ELSE IF, and ELSE, which you've already used in pseudocode and in Scratch's "if/else" blocks. For example: IF grade is greater than or equal to 90 THEN OUTPUT "A" ELSE IF grade is greater than or equal to 80 THEN OUTPUT "B" ELSE OUTPUT "C or below" selects one of three possible outputs, but only one, depending on the value of grade. Iteration means repeating a set of instructions multiple times, using loops like REPEAT or WHILE, which you've seen as Scratch's "repeat" and "forever" blocks. For example: REPEAT 5 TIMES: OUTPUT "Hooray!" would print "Hooray!" five times in a row. Real programs almost always combine all three: a sequence of setup steps, followed by a loop (iteration) that repeats some action, which itself often contains a decision (selection) inside it, like a loop that goes through a list of test scores and, for each one, decides whether it's a passing grade. Recognizing sequencing, selection, and iteration in any piece of code, whether you're reading Scratch blocks, HTML, or soon Python, is like recognizing nouns, verbs, and adjectives in a sentence: it's the basic grammar that every program, no matter how complex, is built from.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Building a Simple Personal Webpage
tasks.content: This lesson brings together everything you've learned about HTML and CSS to build a real, complete project: a simple personal webpage introducing yourself. This is the same basic process professional web developers use every day, just on a smaller scale. Start with the required HTML skeleton: , an tag, a section with a , and a <body> section for the visible content. Inside the body, use an <h1> tag for your name as the main heading, like <h1>Hi, I'm Jordan!</h1>. Follow it with an <h2> for a section like "About Me" and a <p> paragraph underneath describing your hobbies and interests, for example <h2>About Me</h2><p>I love drawing, playing soccer, and reading mystery books.</p>. Add another section, maybe <h2>My Favorite Things</h2>, and consider using more paragraphs or even a link to a website you enjoy, using the <a> tag with an href attribute, like <a href="https://www.nationalgeographic.com">National Geographic</a>. Once your HTML content and structure are complete and correct, add a <style> tag inside your <head> section to bring in CSS and make the page visually yours: change the body's background-color, give your <h1> a distinct color and font-size, and maybe adjust the font-family for your paragraphs to something more personal, like Georgia or Verdana. For example: body { background-color: lightyellow; font-family: Verdana; } h1 { color: darkblue; }. As you build, test frequently by saving your file and reopening it in a browser after every change, rather than writing everything at once and hoping it all works, and use the debugging skills from earlier, checking tag nesting and CSS punctuation, if something doesn't look right. This project isn't just practice, it demonstrates a real, valuable skill: anyone, including you, can now build and publish a genuine webpage using nothing but a text editor and the HTML and CSS you've learned this year.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Studying a novel in depth means tracing how theme, character and historical context interweave across the whole text, not just a single chapter. A character's development often mirrors or challenges a novel's central themes, and understanding when and where a novel was written, its historical context, reveals why certain issues, such as war, class or industrial change, dominate the story. Strong analysis tracks how an author builds a theme gradually, using specific moments and quotations from across the novel rather than relying on a single scene.

tasks.content: A complex sentence combines a main clause, which can stand alone, with one or more subordinate clauses, which cannot, joined by subordinating conjunctions such as 'although,' 'because,' 'while' or 'since.' tasks.content: Every genre carries its own conventions — recognisable features readers expect. Horror relies on building dread through pacing, sensory detail and the unknown; mystery plants clues and red herrings so a reader can almost solve the puzzle alongside the detective; and science fiction extrapolates real science or technology into speculative 'what if' worlds, often to comment on present-day society. Writing convincingly within a genre means deliberately using its conventions — vocabulary, structure, pacing and typical character types — while still creating something original rather than a cliche.

tasks.content: Gothic fiction creates unease through atmosphere as much as plot, typically featuring decaying settings, such as crumbling castles or gloomy mansions, oppressive weather, and a sense of the supernatural or uncanny threatening rational order. Writers build tension through pathetic fallacy, where weather reflects mood, foreshadowing, and withheld information that keeps readers uncertain about what is real. Studying a Gothic extract means tracing exactly how setting, structure and word choice combine to unsettle the reader, rather than simply noting 'it's scary.'

tasks.content: Media literacy means reading news and online content critically, recognising that no source is entirely neutral: headline choice, image selection, which quotations are included, and even word choice, such as 'rioters' versus 'protesters,' can all reveal a publication's bias. Checking a source's ownership, funding and typical audience, and comparing how different outlets report the same story, helps readers spot one-sided reporting and distinguish verified fact from unchecked claims or opinion presented as fact. Being media-literate does not mean distrusting everything — it means questioning and cross-checking before accepting a claim.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A strong argumentative essay states a clear thesis, the writer's central position, in the introduction, then develops distinct points in separate paragraphs, each supported by evidence and explained rather than simply asserted. Acknowledging and rebutting a counter-argument — showing you understand the opposing view before explaining why your position is stronger — makes an argument more persuasive than ignoring it. A confident conclusion restates the thesis in light of the evidence given, without introducing entirely new points.

tasks.content: World literature broadens a reader's understanding beyond the British literary canon, exploring how writers from different countries and cultures use story to explore universal themes — identity, family, conflict, belonging — while also reflecting their own specific cultural and historical context. Reading in translation raises its own questions: a translator makes deliberate choices about word choice, idiom and rhythm, meaning that a translated text carries both the original author's voice and the translator's interpretation. Approaching a text from an unfamiliar culture with curiosity, and researching its context, deepens understanding rather than assuming it works exactly like a familiar British text.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio stays constant, so if y = kx and we know one pair of values we can find k and use it to find others. Two quantities are in inverse proportion if one increases as the other decreases, so xy = k stays constant. For example, if y is directly proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 4, then k = 3, so when x = 9, y = 27.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In a right-angled triangle, Pythagoras' theorem states that a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle). To find the hypotenuse, square both shorter sides, add them, then square root: legs of 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of the square root of (9 + 16) = the square root of 25 = 5. To find a shorter side, rearrange: square the hypotenuse, subtract the known side squared, then square root.

tasks.content: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two variables using plotted points. tasks.content: The digestive system breaks down food into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood and used by the body for energy, growth and repair. Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and saliva start to break down food, continues in the stomach with acid and enzymes, and is completed in the small intestine, where enzymes finish breaking down food and nutrients are absorbed through finger-like projections called villi. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up digestion: amylase breaks down starch into sugars, protease breaks down proteins into amino acids, and lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

tasks.content: In a chemical reaction, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form new substances called products, with new chemical bonds forming; importantly, atoms are never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same, which is known as the law of conservation of mass. Many reactions involve an energy change: exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, often as heat, causing the temperature to rise, while endothermic reactions absorb energy, causing the temperature to fall. Chemical reactions can be represented using word equations and balanced symbol equations, which show exactly how many atoms of each element are involved on both sides.

tasks.content: Electric current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A) with an ammeter, while voltage (potential difference), measured in volts with a voltmeter, is the energy transferred per unit of charge that pushes the current around. Magnets have two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract, with the invisible magnetic field around a magnet mapped using field lines that run from north to south. An electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it, and this effect, called electromagnetism, is used to make electromagnets, which are magnets that can be switched on and off using electricity.

tasks.content: An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms (the community) in an area interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of their environment, such as soil, water and climate. Within an ecosystem, organisms depend on one another through feeding relationships shown in food chains and food webs, where energy passes from producers (usually plants, which make their own food by photosynthesis) to primary consumers, then secondary and tertiary consumers. This interdependence means that a change affecting one species, such as a predator being removed, can have knock-on effects throughout the whole food web, which is why maintaining balanced ecosystems is important.

tasks.content: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number, into rows called periods and columns called groups, with elements in the same group sharing similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. Metals, found on the left and centre of the table, are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable, while non-metals, found on the right, are generally dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors. Group 1 elements, the alkali metals, are very reactive and get more reactive down the group, while Group 0, the noble gases, are extremely unreactive because they already have full outer electron shells.

tasks.content: Energy resources are used to generate the electricity and power we rely on, and are grouped into renewable resources, which are naturally replenished and will not run out, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal and geothermal, and non-renewable resources, such as coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear fuel, which exist in limited amounts and cannot be quickly replaced. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to climate change, while most renewable resources produce little or no carbon dioxide during use but can be less reliable, such as solar power depending on sunlight. Choosing energy resources involves weighing up factors like cost, reliability, environmental impact and how much energy each resource can supply.

tasks.content: Light and sound both travel as waves, but light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum (such as space) at very high speed, while sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrations, which needs a medium like air, water or a solid to travel through, and travels much more slowly. Waves are described using amplitude (the maximum displacement, related to loudness for sound or brightness for light), wavelength (the distance between two matching points on a wave), and frequency (the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz), linked by the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Higher frequency sound waves are heard as higher pitch, while for light, higher frequency corresponds to a different colour, towards the violet/blue end of the visible spectrum.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity, called the reactivity series, which helps predict how they will behave in reactions: more reactive metals, such as potassium and sodium, react vigorously, while less reactive metals, such as gold and copper, are largely unreactive. Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas (more readily for reactive metals), and react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound in a displacement reaction, which is further evidence used to build up the reactivity series.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food, using energy from light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen; it takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy. Respiration, in contrast, occurs in all living cells and releases energy from glucose for the organism to use; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and, in animal cells, produces lactic acid instead. Photosynthesis and respiration are essentially opposite processes, and together they play a key role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Evaluating an investigation means critically reviewing how well the method worked and how confident you can be in the results, rather than simply describing what was done. This includes identifying sources of error, such as random errors (small, unpredictable variations, reduced by repeating measurements and averaging) and systematic errors (a consistent bias, often caused by a fault in equipment such as an incorrectly zeroed balance, which shifts every reading in the same direction). A good evaluation also considers the investigation's reliability (whether repeating it gives consistent results) and validity (whether it actually tests what it claims to, with all other variables properly controlled), and suggests specific, practical improvements.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: புணர்ச்சி (puṇarcci, sandhi) refers to the rules governing how sounds change when two words are joined together in Tamil, similar to how English "do not" becomes "don't." A common example is "மழை" (mazhai, rain) combining with "காலம்" (kaalam, season/time) to form the compound "மழைக்காலம்" (mazhaikkaalam, "rainy season"), where a hard க் sound is inserted at the join. Traditional grammar sorts these changes into categories such as உயிர்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (vowel-to-vowel sandhi), மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (consonant-to-consonant sandhi) and உயிர்மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (mixed sandhi). Recognising sandhi patterns helps you correctly split unfamiliar compound words back into their original parts when reading classical or formal Tamil.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Inbam Pal (இன்பத்துப்பால், also called காமத்துப்பால், Kaamathuppaal) is the third and final section of the Thirukkural, containing 250 couplets across 25 chapters devoted to the theme of இன்பம் (inbam, love). Unlike Aram Pal's ethical teachings or Porul Pal's public-life advice, this section is written as an intimate dialogue between a தலைவன் (thalaivan, hero/lover) and தலைவி (thalaivi, heroine/beloved), exploring courtship, longing, separation and reunion much like the akam poetry of the Sangam tradition. Its verses capture universal emotional experiences of romantic love — the shyness of first attraction, the ache of a lover's absence, the joy of reconciliation — in the same tightly structured two-line kural form used throughout the work. Studying Inbam Pal shows how classical Tamil literature treats love with the same careful craftsmanship as ethics and politics.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka
tasks.content: Tamil history is not only about mainland India — it also includes a long and proud history in இலங்கை (Sri Lanka). Around the 13th century CE, a Tamil kingdom known as the யாழ்ப்பாண இராச்சியம் (Jaffna Kingdom) was established in the northern part of Sri Lanka, ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty. Its capital was நல்லூர் (Nallur), which became an important center of Tamil Hindu (Saiva) culture, religion, and literature in the island. The kingdom built magnificent temples, most famously the நல்லூர் கந்தசுவாமி கோயில் (Nallur Kandaswamy Temple) dedicated to Lord Murugan, which remains one of the most important Hindu temples in Sri Lanka today. The Jaffna Kingdom traded with South India and other parts of the region, and its rulers supported Tamil scholars and poets, helping Tamil language and culture flourish in the north of the island for several centuries. The kingdom remained independent until 1619, when it was conquered by Portuguese colonizers — bringing an end to centuries of Tamil royal rule in Sri Lanka, though Tamil language, culture, and Hindu traditions continued to thrive among the Tamil community there.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This unit follows the central story of Silappathikaram in detail: Kannagi (கண்ணகி) and her husband Kovalan (கோவலன்) are a young married couple from Puhar, but Kovalan falls for a dancer named Madhavi (மாதவி) and squanders his fortune on her before returning, penniless, to Kannagi. The couple travels to Madurai to rebuild their lives, and Kannagi gives Kovalan her silambu (சிலம்பு, anklet) to sell — but he is wrongly accused of stealing the queen's anklet, which looks similar, and is unjustly executed by order of the Pandya king. Grief-stricken, Kannagi marches to the royal court and proves her husband's innocence by breaking open her remaining anklet: hers contains rubies, while the queen's contained pearls. In her fury at this injustice, Kannagi curses the city of Madurai, and this dramatic episode — Kannagi's grief turning to righteous anger — remains one of the most powerful moments in classical Tamil literature.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Kamba Ramayanam (கம்ப ராமாயணம்), also known as Ramavataram (இராமாவதாரம்), is the celebrated Tamil retelling of the Ramayana epic, composed by the poet Kambar (கம்பர்) around the 12th century CE. While it follows the same core story as Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana — Prince Rama's exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, and the eventual war to rescue her — Kambar reshaped the narrative with rich Tamil poetic style, elaborate imagery and emotional depth suited to a Tamil audience of his era. The work is composed in thousands of verses across multiple kandams (books), and Kambar is often praised as one of the greatest poets in the Tamil literary tradition for the sheer craftsmanship of his verse. Kamba Ramayanam remains one of the most celebrated long narrative poems in Tamil literature, distinct in style and detail from its Sanskrit source.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing persuasively about a சமூகப் பிரச்சனை (samoogap pirachanai, social issue) means going beyond simple description to build an argument the reader can be convinced by. Choose a real topic such as சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு (environmental protection) or கல்வியின் முக்கியத்துவம் (the importance of education), then open with a clear thesis stating your position on it. Each body paragraph should present one piece of evidence or reasoning — a statistic, an example, or a logical argument — that directly supports that thesis, rather than simply listing loosely related facts. A strong persuasive essay on a social issue also briefly acknowledges an opposing view before explaining why your position remains stronger, which shows the reader you have thought the issue through carefully.

tasks.content: Building on the introduction to debate from Grade 6, this unit practises the formal roles and structure used in a organised Tamil வாதப் போட்டி (vaadhap potti, debate competition). Each side has a முன்மொழிபவர் (munmozhibavar, proposer) who opens the case, and speakers alternate presenting points within a strict கால வரம்பு (kaala varambu, time limit) enforced by a நடுவர் (naduvar, judge/adjudicator). A well-prepared formal debater doesn't just state opinions but organises them into a clear கட்டமைப்பு (kattamaippu, structure) — point, evidence, and a brief rebuttal of the opposing side's likely argument — delivered confidently within the time allowed. Practising this formal structure under timed conditions builds the confidence needed for real competitive debating.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced translation goes beyond simple sentences to tackle idiomatic expressions, where a literal, word-for-word translation would sound strange or lose the original meaning entirely. For example, the Tamil proverb "கிணற்றுத் தவளைக்குக் கடல் தெரியுமா?" should not be translated literally as "does the well's frog know the ocean" but rendered with its equivalent English idiom, "like a frog in a well," to preserve the intended meaning for an English reader. Similarly, translating longer, more complex sentences requires reordering clauses — a Tamil sentence with a relative participle (பெயரெச்சம்) placed before a noun, like "நேற்று வந்த மாணவன்" (the student who came yesterday), must be restructured into an English relative clause with "who," since English cannot place a whole clause directly before a noun in the same way. Skilled translators balance staying faithful to the original meaning with producing natural, fluent sentences in the target language.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Puthukavithai (புதுக்கவிதை, "new poetry") is the modern free-verse movement in Tamil poetry that emerged in the 20th century as a deliberate break from the strict yaappu (poetic meter) rules that had shaped Tamil verse for centuries. Instead of fixed metrical patterns and rhyme, puthukavithai poets write in free verse, using natural rhythms of spoken Tamil, everyday vocabulary and contemporary themes — city life, personal emotion, social commentary — that older classical forms rarely addressed directly. This shift mirrors similar free-verse movements in other world literatures, where poets prioritised emotional directness and thematic freedom over rigid formal constraints. Reading puthukavithai alongside classical Sangam or Thirukkural verse highlights just how dramatically Tamil poetic form has evolved while the language itself remains continuous.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Functions in Python: Reusable Code
tasks.content: A function in Python is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task, similar to a procedure but with an important extra feature: a function can send a value back to whatever called it. A function is created using the def keyword, followed by a chosen name and round brackets, which may contain parameters, values passed into the function to use. For example: def greet(name): print("Hello, " + name) defines a function called greet that takes one parameter, name; calling greet("Amy") runs the indented code inside, printing Hello, Amy. Many functions also use the return keyword to send a result back, rather than just printing something directly. For example: def add(a, b): return a + b defines a function that calculates a sum and returns it; writing result = add(3, 4) then print(result) stores the returned value 7 in result and displays it. This matters because a returned value can be stored, compared, or used again elsewhere in the program, whereas something merely printed inside a function cannot be reused afterwards. If a function has no return statement, Python still gives it a result automatically: the special value None, meaning nothing was explicitly returned. Functions bring the same benefits as procedures, avoiding repeated code and making programs easier to read and test, but the ability to return values makes them especially powerful for calculations, since a function like square(n), returning n * n, can be reused anywhere a squared number is needed, keeping the main program short, clear, and focused on what should happen rather than exactly how each calculation is performed.

levels.levelName: Lists and Data Structures in Python

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Lists and Data Structures in Python
tasks.content: A list is a data structure in Python used to store an ordered collection of items together in a single variable, rather than needing a separate variable for every value. A list is created using square brackets, with items separated by commas, for example fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] creates a list of three strings. Each item in a list has a position, called an index, and Python indexing starts counting from 0, not 1, so fruits[0] refers to "apple", the first item, and fruits[1] refers to "banana". A negative index counts from the end of the list, so fruits[-1] refers to the last item, "cherry", which is useful when the exact length of a list is not known. The len() function returns how many items are in a list, so len(fruits) returns 3. Lists are mutable, meaning their contents can be changed after creation: nums = [10, 20, 30], then nums[1] = 99, changes the list to [10, 99, 30], replacing the item at index 1. New items can be added to the end of a list using the append() method, so fruits.append("date") changes the list to ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'date']. Lists work naturally with for loops, since for f in fruits: print(f) will run once for every item in the list, automatically printing each fruit on its own line without needing to know in advance how many items the list contains. Storing related data together in a list, rather than in many separate variables, makes programs far easier to manage, especially when the amount of data might grow or shrink while a program runs.

tasks.content: A string is a sequence of characters, and Python provides many built-in tools for examining and transforming strings, which is especially useful when working with user input or text data. Like a list, each character in a string has an index starting from 0, so for s = "Hello World", s[0] gives "H" and s[-1] gives the last character, "d". The len() function also works on strings, counting every character including spaces, so len(s) for "Hello World" returns 11. Strings have several useful built-in methods, called by adding a full stop after the string followed by the method name. The .upper() method returns a new version of the string in capital letters, so s.upper() returns "HELLO WORLD", while .lower() does the opposite, converting to lower case. The .split() method breaks a string into a list of smaller strings, dividing at a chosen character, most often a space; s.split(" ") on "Hello World" returns the list ["Hello", "World"], which is very useful for processing sentences word by word. The .replace() method searches for one piece of text within a string and swaps it for another, so s.replace("World", "Python") returns "Hello Python", leaving the original string in s unchanged unless the result is stored back into a variable. Strings can also be joined together, or concatenated, using the plus sign, so "Hello" + " " + "World" produces "Hello World". It is important to remember that these methods do not change the original string in place; Python strings are immutable, so each method call produces a brand new string, which must be stored in a variable if it needs to be kept and used later.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Boolean Logic and Truth Tables
tasks.content: Boolean logic deals with values that can only be True or False, and it underlies every decision a computer makes, from a simple if statement to the design of the circuits inside a CPU. Three fundamental logical operators combine or change these values: AND, OR and NOT. The AND operator produces True only when both of its inputs are True; in Python, True and False evaluates to False, since one input is False. The OR operator produces True when at least one of its inputs is True; True or False evaluates to True, because at least one side is True. The NOT operator simply reverses a single value; not True evaluates to False, and not False evaluates to True. A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and shows the resulting output, which is a clear way to fully describe how a logical operator behaves. For AND, with inputs A and B, the table shows: 0 and 0 gives 0, 0 and 1 gives 0, 1 and 0 gives 0, and only 1 and 1 gives 1, using 1 for True and 0 for False. For OR, the table shows: 0 or 0 gives 0, but 0 or 1, 1 or 0, and 1 or 1 all give 1, since only one input needs to be True. These simple rules are combined to build more complex conditions in programs, such as checking that a password is both long enough and contains a number, which would use AND, or checking that a user is either an administrator or a verified member, which would use OR. The same logic gates, built from electronic circuits, are also the basic building blocks used inside a CPU to perform arithmetic and make decisions at the hardware level.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Representing Text, Images and Sound in Binary

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Representing Text, Images and Sound in Binary
tasks.content: Every type of data a computer handles, whatever it looks or sounds like to a human, is ultimately stored as patterns of binary digits, using agreed coding systems that both the computer and its software understand. Text is represented using character sets, which assign a unique binary code to every letter, digit and symbol. The older ASCII system uses patterns of bits to represent English letters, digits and basic punctuation, so, for example, the capital letter 'A' is represented by the denary value 65, which is 01000001 in binary; because it only supports a limited number of characters, modern systems increasingly use Unicode instead, which uses more bits to represent a vastly larger range of characters, including accented letters, non-Latin alphabets and emoji, from many of the world's languages. Images are represented as a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels; the more pixels used, called the resolution, the more detailed the image can be. Each pixel's colour is itself stored in binary, commonly using 8 bits for each of red, green and blue, called colour depth, giving 24 bits per pixel and allowing over 16 million possible colours; higher resolution and greater colour depth both produce better quality images but also significantly larger file sizes. Sound is represented by sampling: a microphone or sound wave is measured, and its amplitude at each moment is recorded as a binary number, many times every second. The sample rate is how many samples are taken per second, and the sample resolution, or bit depth, is how many bits are used to store each sample; increasing either produces a more accurate recreation of the original sound but also increases the file size considerably.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: How the CPU Executes Instructions
tasks.content: The central processing unit constantly repeats a process called the fetch-decode-execute cycle in order to run every program, from a simple calculator app to a full operating system. First, in the fetch stage, the CPU retrieves the next instruction from memory, using a special register called the Program Counter to keep track of which instruction should be fetched next, and the Memory Address Register and Memory Data Register to locate and collect that instruction from RAM. Next, in the decode stage, the instruction is translated so the CPU understands exactly what operation it represents and what data, if any, it needs. Finally, in the execute stage, the CPU actually carries out the instruction, which might involve a calculation, moving data, or making a decision, often using a register called the Accumulator to store the result. This entire cycle then repeats for the next instruction, happening billions of times every second in a modern computer. The speed at which this cycle repeats is measured by the clock speed, given in Hertz (Hz), or more commonly gigahertz (GHz) for modern processors, where one gigahertz means one billion cycles per second; a higher clock speed generally allows more instructions to be processed every second, making the computer perform tasks faster, although it is not the only factor affecting performance. Many modern CPUs also contain multiple cores, essentially several separate processing units built into a single chip, allowing genuinely different tasks, or parts of the same task, to be worked on at the same time, called parallel processing. CPUs also use a small amount of extremely fast memory called cache, positioned very close to the processor, to store frequently used data and instructions so they can be accessed far more quickly than fetching the same information from RAM every single time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: The Internet: Protocols and the World Wide Web

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Internet: Protocols and the World Wide Web
tasks.content: Although the terms are often used interchangeably, the internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing. The internet is the huge, physical network of networks connecting devices worldwide, while the World Wide Web is a service that runs on top of the internet, made up of linked web pages and websites accessed through a browser; email, online gaming and video calls also run over the internet but are not part of the Web itself. For all these services to work reliably, devices must agree on protocols, which are sets of rules that define exactly how data should be formatted, sent and received, so that different devices and software, even from different manufacturers, can communicate successfully. The Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, is responsible for breaking data into packets before sending, checking that every packet arrives correctly, and reassembling them in the right order at the destination, requesting any missing packets again if needed. The Internet Protocol, or IP, works alongside TCP, handling addressing and making sure each packet is routed toward the correct destination device based on its IP address; together these are often referred to as TCP/IP. For browsing the Web specifically, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, or HTTP, defines how a browser requests a web page and how a server responds with that page's content; HTTPS is a more secure version of the same protocol, encrypting the data exchanged so that anyone intercepting it cannot easily read it, which is essential whenever sensitive information, such as passwords or payment details, is being sent. Other protocols handle other tasks, such as FTP for transferring files between computers, showing that the smooth operation of the internet actually depends on many different, carefully agreed protocols working correctly together.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Cyber Security: Threats and Protections
tasks.content: Cyber security is the practice of protecting computer systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or theft, and understanding common threats is the first step toward defending against them. Phishing remains one of the most common threats: fraudulent messages or websites designed to trick people into revealing personal information, such as passwords or bank details, by pretending to be a trustworthy source. Weak or reused passwords are another major risk, since a password that is easy to guess, or used across multiple accounts, gives an attacker who cracks or steals it access to far more than intended. Unpatched software, meaning software that has not been updated with the latest security fixes, can also leave a serious weakness that attackers are able to exploit, since software companies regularly release updates specifically to close newly discovered security gaps. Fortunately, several protections exist to defend against these threats. A firewall monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic, using a set of rules to block suspicious or unauthorised connections before they can reach a device or network. Anti-malware software scans files and programs for known malicious code, removing or blocking anything harmful it detects. Encryption scrambles data using a mathematical process so that it becomes unreadable to anyone without the correct key to decode it, protecting information even if it is intercepted or stolen. Keeping software updated ensures that known security weaknesses are patched as quickly as possible. Finally, strong authentication, including well-chosen passwords and two-factor authentication, makes it significantly harder for an unauthorised person to gain access, even if some information about an account has already been leaked or guessed.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: Copyright and Ownership of Digital Content

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Copyright and Ownership of Digital Content
tasks.content: Copyright is a legal protection that automatically applies to original creative work as soon as it is created, without needing to be registered or marked in any special way, and it applies just as much to digital content as to physical work. This means that text, images, music, videos, and even computer program code found online are very likely protected by copyright, owned by whoever created them, even if no copyright symbol or notice is visible on the page. Copyright generally gives the creator control over how their work is copied, distributed, or used by others, so downloading an image from the internet and using it in a school project, a video, or a website without permission may infringe that creator's rights, even if no money changes hands and even if it seems like a small or harmless use. This is different from, but related to, plagiarism, which specifically means presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own, without giving them credit; it is possible to plagiarise work that is not protected by copyright at all, and possible to breach copyright while still crediting the original creator, since credit alone does not always grant legal permission to use something. Some creators choose to release their work under a Creative Commons licence, a system that allows them to permit certain uses of their work in advance, such as free use for non-commercial projects as long as the creator is credited, making it much easier for others to find and legally reuse online content. Software is protected similarly through software licences: proprietary software restricts copying, modifying, and redistributing the code, while open-source software is deliberately shared under a licence that allows anyone to view, use, and often modify and redistribute its code, provided the licence's conditions are followed.

levels.levelName: Creating a Digital Artefact: Project Work

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Creating a Digital Artefact: Project Work
tasks.content: This unit brings together a year's worth of computing skills by planning, building and evaluating a complete digital artefact, such as a small website, an animation, a database, or a piece of software, chosen to solve a genuine problem or meet a real need for an intended audience. The project follows a clear life cycle. First comes analysis, where the requirements of the task are identified clearly: what the artefact needs to do, who it is for, and what would count as success. Next comes design, where the solution is planned before any building begins, using tools such as storyboards, wireframes, flowcharts or written plans, and where the problem is decomposed into smaller, manageable parts. During development, the artefact is actually created, ideally building and testing it in stages rather than all at once, so that problems are caught and fixed while they are still small and easy to trace back to their cause. Testing then checks the finished artefact thoroughly against the original requirements identified during analysis, using a range of realistic inputs and, where possible, feedback from other people trying it out, since a creator can easily overlook problems that a new user notices immediately. Finally, evaluation looks back honestly at the whole project: does the finished artefact actually meet the original need, what went well, what could be improved, and what would be done differently next time. Working through this full cycle, rather than jumping straight to development, mirrors how real digital products are built professionally, and reinforces that good computing work depends as much on careful planning, testing and reflection as it does on the code or content produced.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Python Syntax: print() and Comments
tasks.content: Welcome to Python, one of the most popular programming languages in the world, used for everything from websites and video games to scientific research and artificial intelligence. Unlike Scratch, where you dragged blocks, Python programs are entirely typed as text, which means precision matters: correct spelling, correct punctuation, and even correct spacing all affect whether your code works. The very first thing most people learn in any new language is how to display a message on the screen, and in Python, you do this with the print() function: print("Hello, world!") will output the exact text Hello, world! to the screen when the program runs. Notice a few important details: the text you want to display goes inside parentheses, and it must be wrapped in quotation marks, either single ('like this') or double ("like this"), which tells Python "this is text, not a command." This kind of text, wrapped in quotes, is called a string. You can print as many lines as you like by using print() multiple times: print("Hello!") followed by print("Welcome to Python.") will show two separate lines of output, one after another, because each print() automatically starts a new line after it finishes. Just as important as print() are comments, which are notes written directly in your code that Python completely ignores when running the program. In Python, anything after a hashtag symbol # on a line is a comment, like # This program greets the user. Comments don't affect how your program runs at all; they exist purely to help humans, including your future self, understand what a piece of code is doing or why it was written that way. Good programmers use comments to explain tricky logic, leave reminders, or temporarily "turn off" a line of code while testing, by putting a # in front of it. Getting comfortable with print() and comments from the very start builds the habit of writing code that is not just correct, but clear and readable for anyone who looks at it later.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Variables and Data Types in Python
tasks.content: A variable in Python is a name that stores a value so you can use and change it later in your program, and you create one simply by writing a name, an equals sign, and a value, like age = 12. Here, "age" is the variable name, and 12 is the value stored inside it; from then on, using "age" anywhere in your code refers to that stored value. Unlike Scratch, where you clicked "Make a Variable" and picked a name from a list of blocks, in Python you create variables just by assigning them, and you can change their value anytime by writing a new assignment, like age = 13. Python organizes values into different data types, and the three most important ones to know right now are integers, floats, and strings. An integer, or int, is a whole number with no decimal point, like 12 or -5. A float is a number with a decimal point, like 3.14 or 98.6, used whenever you need more precision than a whole number allows. A string, which you saw in the last lesson, is text wrapped in quotation marks, like "hello" or "Jordan." Python is smart about telling these apart: name = "Maria" creates a string, while score = 95 creates an integer, and temperature = 98.6 creates a float, all without you needing to say directly which type you want. You can combine variables with print() to display personalized messages, like name = "Sam" followed by print("Hello, " + name), which outputs Hello, Sam by joining, or "concatenating," two strings together with the plus sign. It's important to know that you generally can't mix types carelessly: trying to add a string directly to a number, like "Score: " + 95, will cause an error, because Python doesn't automatically know whether you mean to combine text or do math; you would need to convert the number to a string first using str(95). Understanding variables and data types is the foundation for almost everything else you'll do in Python.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In the last two grades, you used "if/else" logic in Scratch blocks and in pseudocode, and now you'll write it as real Python code, using the keywords if, elif, and else. An if statement checks a condition, and if that condition is True, it runs the indented code underneath it. For example: age = 15, followed by if age >= 13: print("You are a teenager"), will print "You are a teenager" because 15 is indeed greater than or equal to 13. Notice two very important Python rules here: the line with "if" ends in a colon (:), and the code that should run when the condition is true must be indented, usually with four spaces, underneath it; Python uses this indentation, rather than curly braces or "end" words, to know which lines belong inside the if statement. When you have more than two possibilities, you use elif, short for "else if," to check additional conditions in order, and else to catch anything that didn't match any earlier condition. For example: score = 85, if score >= 90: print("A"), elif score >= 80: print("B"), elif score >= 70: print("C"), else: print("Needs improvement"). Here, Python checks each condition from top to bottom, and score = 85 fails the first check (85 is not >= 90) but passes the second (85 is >= 80), so it prints "B" and skips the rest, even though 85 also happens to be >= 70. This top-to-bottom, first-match-wins behavior is important: order your elif conditions carefully, because once one matches, Python stops checking the rest. Comparison operators used inside these conditions include == (equal to, note the double equals sign, different from a single = used for assignment), != (not equal to), >, <, >=, and <=. Mastering if/elif/else is essential because almost every real program needs to make decisions based on changing information, whether it's checking a login password, sorting scores into letter grades, or deciding what a game character should do next.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A for loop in Python lets you repeat an action a specific number of times, or once for every item in a collection, similar to Scratch's "repeat" block but far more flexible. The most common way to repeat something a set number of times uses the range() function, like this: for i in range(5): print("Hooray!"), which prints "Hooray!" exactly five times, once for each number range(5) produces: 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Notice that range(5) starts counting at 0 and stops before reaching 5, giving exactly five numbers total, which can be surprising at first but is an important rule to remember in Python. The variable "i" in "for i in range(5)" is called the loop variable, and it changes value on each pass through the loop, so you can actually use it inside the loop, like for i in range(5): print(i), which prints 0, 1, 2, 3, then 4, each on its own line. For loops are also perfect for going through every item in a list, using a pattern like: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"], for fruit in fruits: print(fruit), which prints each fruit's name on its own line, apple, then banana, then cherry, without you needing to know how many items are in the list ahead of time. This is exactly the "for each" idea you learned about with Scratch lists, now written as real Python code. Just like if statements, for loops require a colon at the end of the "for" line, and the code that should repeat must be indented underneath it; anything not indented is considered outside the loop and only runs once, after the loop finishes. A common beginner mistake is forgetting that range(5) doesn't include 5, or forgetting the colon and indentation, both of which cause errors or unexpected behavior. For loops are one of the most-used tools in all of programming, letting you process lists of data, repeat calculations, and build patterns with just a few lines of code.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a certain condition stays True, which makes it different from a for loop that typically repeats a set number of times or once per item in a list. A while loop is perfect for situations where you don't know in advance exactly how many times you'll need to repeat, like asking a user to keep guessing a number until they get it right. The basic pattern looks like this: count = 0, while count < 5: print(count), count = count + 1. This prints 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, one per line, and then stops, because each time through the loop, count increases by 1, and once count reaches 5, the condition "count < 5" becomes False, so the loop ends. This last step, updating the variable being checked, is absolutely critical: if you forgot the line "count = count + 1," the condition "count < 5" would stay True forever, since count would always equal 0, and your program would run in what's called an infinite loop, repeating forever and likely freezing or crashing your program. This is one of the most common mistakes beginners make with while loops, so always double check that something inside the loop is actually working toward making the condition eventually False. While loops are especially useful for input validation, repeatedly asking a user for information until they provide something valid, like: guess = -1, while guess != 7: guess = int(input("Guess the number: ")), which keeps asking "Guess the number:" over and over until the user finally types 7. Just like if statements and for loops, while loops require a colon after the condition and indentation for the code that repeats. Understanding when to use a for loop, when you know the number of repetitions or are working through a list, versus a while loop, when you're repeating based on a condition that might take an unknown number of tries, is an important decision every Python programmer makes constantly.

tasks.content: So far your programs have used fixed values written directly into the code, but real programs usually need to react to whatever the person using them types in, and Python makes this easy with the input() function. Writing name = input("What is your name? ") does two things at once: it displays the text "What is your name? " on the screen as a prompt, then pauses the program and waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and whatever they typed gets stored as a string inside the variable "name." You can then use that variable just like any other, for example print("Hello, " + name + "!"), which would greet the user by whatever name they entered. Here's a critically important rule to remember: input() always returns a string, even if the user types numbers. This means if you write age = input("How old are you? ") and the user types 12, the variable age actually holds the string "12," not the integer 12, and trying to do math with it directly, like age + 1, would cause an error, because you can't add a number to a string. To fix this, you need to convert the input using int(), like age = int(input("How old are you? ")), which converts the typed text into a real integer so you can then safely do things like print(age + 1) to correctly show 13. If the value might include a decimal, like a price or height, you'd use float() instead of int() to convert it. A simple full example: name = input("What is your name? "), age = int(input("How old are you? ")), print(name + " will turn " + str(age + 1) + " next year."), which combines a string input, a converted integer input, and converting a number back into a string with str() so it can be joined with other text. Getting comfortable with input(), and remembering to convert it to int() or float() whenever you need to do math, is essential for building any interactive Python program, including the calculator project coming up soon.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A function in Python is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task, and it's directly related to the custom blocks you built in Scratch, just written as real code now. You've actually already been using functions this whole time: print() and input() are both built-in Python functions. Now you'll learn to write your own. A function is created using the keyword def (short for "define"), followed by the function's name, parentheses, and a colon, with the function's code indented underneath, just like if statements and loops. For example: def greet(): print("Hello!") print("Welcome to Python.") defines a function called greet that, whenever it's called, prints two lines. Importantly, defining a function doesn't run it; you have to call it by writing its name followed by parentheses, like greet(), for the code inside to actually execute. Functions become much more powerful with parameters, inputs you can pass in to change how the function behaves each time, similar to the parameters you used in Scratch custom blocks. For example: def greet(name): print("Hello, " + name + "!"), and then calling greet("Maria") prints "Hello, Maria!" while calling greet("Alex") prints "Hello, Alex!", using the exact same function definition but different input each time. Functions can also send a value back to whoever called them using the return keyword: def add(a, b): return a + b, and then writing result = add(3, 4) stores the value 7 in the variable "result," because the function calculated 3 + 4 and returned it. Notice the difference between print() inside a function, which just displays something on screen, and return, which actually hands a value back so it can be stored, used in more calculations, or passed to other functions. Writing functions makes your programs organized, reusable, and much easier to test and fix, because instead of one giant block of code, you have small, clearly named, independent pieces, each responsible for doing exactly one job well.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Python code, unlike Scratch blocks, can fail to run at all if there's even a small mistake, and Python will usually respond with an error message called a "traceback," which tells you what kind of problem occurred and on which line. Learning to read these messages, rather than fearing them, is one of the most valuable debugging skills you can build. There are three broad categories of bugs to know. A syntax error happens when your code breaks Python's grammar rules, like forgetting a colon after an if statement, forgetting a closing parenthesis, or misspelling a keyword; Python catches these before your program even starts running and will point to roughly where the problem is. A runtime error happens while the program is running and something goes wrong partway through, like trying to divide by zero, or trying to do math with a string that hasn't been converted with int(), which causes a TypeError; Python stops the program right at that line and shows you the error type and a description. The trickiest kind is a logic error, where your code runs perfectly fine, with no error messages at all, but produces the wrong result because the logic itself is flawed, like writing "if score > 90" when you meant "if score >= 90," accidentally excluding a score of exactly 90 from getting an A. Since logic errors don't cause visible errors, finding them requires actively testing your program with different inputs and checking whether the output matches what you expect. A powerful debugging technique for all three types is adding temporary print() statements at key points in your code, like print("age is:", age), to see the actual value of a variable at that moment, which often reveals exactly where your assumption about the code's behavior was wrong. Reading error messages carefully, checking indentation and colons, converting input types correctly, and testing with a variety of inputs are the core habits that will make you a confident, capable Python debugger.

tasks.content: It's time to combine everything you've learned this year, print(), variables, if/elif/else, input(), type conversion, and functions, into one complete project: a simple text-based calculator. The goal is a program that asks the user for two numbers and an operation, then performs the correct calculation and displays the result. Start by planning with pseudocode: START, INPUT first number, INPUT second number, INPUT operation (+, -, *, or /), IF operation is + THEN result is first plus second, ELIF operation is - THEN result is first minus second, ELIF operation is * THEN result is first times second, ELIF operation is / THEN result is first divided by second, OUTPUT result, END. Translating this into Python, you'd first collect the numbers using input(), remembering to convert them with float() so decimals work and math is possible: num1 = float(input("Enter the first number: ")), num2 = float(input("Enter the second number: ")), operation = input("Enter an operation (+, -, *, /): "). Then use if/elif/else to check which operation was chosen and calculate accordingly: if operation == "+": result = num1 + num2, elif operation == "-": result = num1 - num2, elif operation == "*": result = num1 * num2, elif operation == "/": result = num1 / num2, else: print("Invalid operation"). Finally, display the answer with print("The result is: " + str(result)), remembering to convert the number back into a string with str() so it can be joined with text. For an extra challenge, wrap the whole calculator in a function called calculate(), or even a while loop that lets the user perform multiple calculations without restarting the program, stopping only when they type something like "quit." A well-built calculator should also consider the edge case of dividing by zero, since real division by zero causes a runtime error in Python; a more advanced version might check "if operation == '/' and num2 == 0: print('Cannot divide by zero')" before attempting the division. Building this calculator proves you can combine input, decisions, and output into one working, interactive Python program from start to finish.

tasks.content: You've now completed your first full year of real Python programming, moving from simple print() statements all the way to variables, decisions, loops, user input, and functions, ending with a working calculator project. This final review lesson looks back at everything and combines it into one more complete mini project: a simple number-guessing game. Start, as always, with pseudocode: START, choose a secret number, set guesses to 0, REPEAT: ask the player to guess a number, add 1 to guesses, IF guess equals secret number THEN print "You got it!" and STOP, ELIF guess is less than secret number THEN print "Too low", ELSE print "Too high", END REPEAT, OUTPUT how many guesses it took, END. Translating this into Python combines nearly every concept from this year: a variable to hold the secret number, secret = 7 (or generated randomly using Python's random module with random.randint(1, 20)); a variable guesses = 0 to track attempts; a while loop, since you don't know in advance how many guesses it will take, using a condition like while True combined with an if/elif/else chain and a break statement to exit once the guess is correct; input() combined with int() to safely collect and convert each guess; and print() combined with str() or Python's comma-separated print syntax to show helpful feedback and the final results. You could also wrap parts of this game in a function, like def check_guess(guess, secret): return guess == secret, to keep your code organized and reusable, exactly the same instinct you practiced with custom blocks back in Scratch. As you build, apply your debugging skills: read error messages carefully if the program crashes, add temporary print() statements to check variable values if the logic seems wrong, and test with multiple different secret numbers and guess patterns to make sure every path, guessing too high, too low, and correctly, works as expected. Completing this project is proof that the core ideas you've been building since Scratch, sequence, selection, iteration, variables, and now functions, are the exact same ideas powering real, professional Python programs, and you're ready to build even more with them next year.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: At the highest level, creative writing is a series of deliberate choices: every word, and every sentence's length and structure, should be chosen for a specific effect rather than habit. Precise verbs and concrete nouns, such as 'the branch snapped' rather than 'something happened,' create sharper images than vague, general language, while sentence length can be manipulated to control pacing — a sudden short sentence after a long, flowing one can land like a physical jolt. Strong writers redraft deliberately, questioning each word choice: does this verb, this rhythm, this structure serve the effect I want the reader to feel?

tasks.content: Transactional writing produces a text with a genuine real-world purpose and audience — a formal letter of complaint, a speech to persuade an audience, or a magazine article to inform and entertain — and each form has its own conventions of layout, tone and structure. Other methods include random sampling (every member has an equal chance) and systematic sampling (selecting every nth item from a list).

Real-life graphs such as distance-time graphs also carry meaning: a horizontal section means the object is stationary, and the gradient of a sloped section represents speed.

tasks.content: Genetic information is stored in the nucleus of a cell in structures called chromosomes, made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), which is coiled into a double helix shape; sections of DNA that code for particular characteristics are called genes. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs in most body cells, having inherited one chromosome of each pair from each parent, while cells divide by mitosis to produce two identical new cells for growth and repair. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, which can have different versions called alleles, and whether a dominant or recessive allele is expressed determines the characteristic (phenotype) an organism shows.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Atoms are made of three types of subatomic particle: protons and neutrons, which have relatively large mass and are found in the central nucleus, and electrons, which have almost no mass and orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels); protons carry a positive charge, electrons a negative charge, and neutrons no charge, and in a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons. The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number, which identifies the element, while the total number of protons and neutrons is its mass number. Atoms bond together in different ways: ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons between a metal and a non-metal to form charged ions that attract each other, covalent bonding involves non-metal atoms sharing pairs of electrons, and metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Pressure is the force acting per unit area, calculated with the formula pressure = force ÷ area, and measured in pascals (Pa); this is why a sharp knife (small area) cuts more easily than a blunt one with the same force, and why wide skis spread a person's weight over a larger area to reduce pressure on snow. Pressure in a fluid, such as in a liquid, increases with depth because of the increasing weight of fluid above, and acts equally in all directions at a given point. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces affect movement: an object stays still or moves at a constant speed unless acted on by an unbalanced force (Newton's first law), and the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, F = ma (Newton's second law).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The rate of a chemical reaction describes how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed, and can be increased by raising the temperature (giving particles more energy so they collide more often and harder), increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas (making collisions more frequent), increasing the surface area of a solid reactant (exposing more particles to collide with), or adding a catalyst, which speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. This is explained by collision theory: for a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy, called the activation energy, and more frequent or more energetic collisions lead to a faster reaction rate. Rate of reaction can be measured experimentally, for example by timing how long it takes for a fixed amount of gas to be produced, or by measuring how a reaction mixture's mass or appearance changes over time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body, such as temperature, water content and blood glucose levels, to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes outside the body. The nervous system detects and responds to changes (stimuli) rapidly using electrical signals: receptors detect a stimulus, sensory neurones carry signals to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), which processes information and sends signals along motor neurones to effectors, such as muscles or glands, which produce a response. A reflex is an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, protecting the body from harm, such as pulling your hand away from something hot.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electrical power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (W), and can be calculated using the equation power = voltage × current (P = V × I); a higher-power appliance transfers more energy every second. In a series circuit, current is the same at every point and the total voltage is shared between components, whereas in a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same, but the current is shared between branches, so removing one component does not stop current flowing through the others. Energy transferred by an electrical appliance can be calculated using energy = power × time, which is how domestic electricity bills, based on the number of kilowatt-hours used, are calculated.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based compounds, most of which are found in or derived from living things or fossil fuels; carbon atoms can form up to four covalent bonds, allowing them to build long chains and rings, giving rise to a huge variety of organic molecules. Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of hydrogen and carbon atoms, and crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, most of which belong to a family called alkanes; alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2 and contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, making them relatively unreactive (saturated). Crude oil is separated into more useful fractions, such as petrol, diesel and kerosene, by fractional distillation, which separates hydrocarbons based on their different boiling points.
